It consists of a large block of wood, suspended from a strong horizontal axis; and it is so solidly constructed as to bear the heaviest blow of the heaviest shot without injury. An excavated centre on one side of the block is tilled with sand, packed in leather upon an iron frame; four bags form a filling or core. The core, forming the place of impact, is easily replaced after each tiring. Straps of wrought iron suspend the block from the wrought- iron axis or shaft. The shaft-ends have knife- which rest on V supports. The construction is such, that a violent percussion makes only a very slight oscillatory movement in the block. A brass graduated limb measures the arc of vibration ; and a brass slide is pushed forward by an index attached to a bar connected with the suspension straps. Another form of instrument for similar purposes will be described under Eprouvettk ; and some of the results of these experiments will be noticed under Cinnery. See War-Services in Supp.

balloon.c:
BALLOON (Fr. ballon, a large ball). According to the principle of Archimedes (q. v.), bodies immersed in a fluid are buoyed upwards with a force equivalent to the weight of the fluid displaced by them. If their own weight is not sufficient to counterbalance

this force — that is, if they are lighter than the Huid — they rise upwards with a force equal to the difference of the weight of the displaced fluid, and of their own weight. A B., therefore, which consists of an integument enclosing a gas within it, will rise in air Balloon. in the same way that a cork rises in water, provided that the weight of the whole be less than that of an equal volume of air. If one, for instance, occupy as much space as 1000 lbs. of air, but weigh itself — covering, gas, and appendages — COO lbs., it will be impelled upwards with a force of 400 lbs. The gases employed for killing balloons are either hydrogen or ordinary coal-gas. The former, when pure, is between fourteen and fifteen times lighter than atmospheric air, and the latter generally about two and a half. The B., as it is at present employed, is a large pear-shaped bag, made of any pliable sdk cloth, covered with a varnish, made by dissolving caoutchouc in oil of turpentine, to render it air-tight. The common size of this bag varies from 20 to 30 feet in equatorial diameter with a proportionate height. The mouth or neck of this bag is just large enough to enable a man to get inside to make any necessary repairs, and is, of course, turned downwards when the B. is inflated. A net-work of hempen or cotton twine is accurately fitted to Che I'., and the separate cords, on which it ends, are tied to a circular hoop placed a few feet below the neck. The car, generally a large wicker- baskst, is suspended by ropes from this hoop, and 1 1 at a considerable distance below, so that the laut may be removed from the vicinity of the gas. The net-work serves to distribute the weight of the ear and its charge equally over the whole upper surface of the balloon. One of the most important requisites in the construction is the valve, which is introduced into the top of the balloon. It consists of a wooden clapper, four or five inches square, opening inwards, and kept closed by a suiiicient spring. A rope attached to this valve descends through the neck into the ear, where, to prevent accidental opening , it is allowed to dangle freely. The furniture of the car are the ballast or sand-bags, by emptying ■which the B. may bo lightened : the barometer, or corresponding apparatus for telling the ascended, or the upward or downward course of the B. ; the map and compass, for shewing the direction of the voyage ; and the grappling-iron, tied to the end of a long rope, for anchoring the B. at the descent. During his flight, the aeronaut has at his al the means of guiding his air-ship only in an upward or dowin. n, the motion of translation being wholly dependent on the wind by which it is borne. If he wishes to ascend, he throws some of the ballast over the side of the car ; and if to descend, he pulls the valve-rope, so that, the gas rushing by virtue of its specific lightness through the passage made for it by the open valve, the buoyant material may be lessened. It is evident that the power of thus directing his machine becomes more limited with each exercise of it, for in each case there is an unrepaired loss of the means necessary to it. All attempts at guiding balloons in a horizontal direction have hitherto proved failures. In ordinary flights, the mouth of the B. is left open, so that there is no danger of explosion arising from the expansion of the the rarer regions of the atmosphere. The dii that takes place through the open neck is inconsiderable during the few hours that an aerial voyage lasts. Early aeronauts, who kept their balloons closed, frequently ran considerable risk by inattention to the valve when the imprisoned gas demanded vent for its expansion. The art of traversing the air by means of balloons, generally called Aeronautics, and sometimes Aerostation , is of comparatively recent date. The germ of the invention of balloons is to be found in the discovery by Cavendish, in 1766, of the remarkable lightness of hydrogen gas, then called inflammable air. Professor Black, of Edinburgh, seems to have been the first who conceived the idea that a light envelope, containing this gas, would rise of i He requested Dr Monro, the professor of anatomy, to give him some thin animal membrane for the experiment, but for some reason or other, it was never made. The first practical attempts were made by C'avallo, who, in 1772, filled swine's bladders and paper-bags with the gas, but found the former too heavy, aud the latter too porous ; and he only succeeded in raising soap-bubbles inflated with the The invention of the B. is due to the two brothers Stephen and Joseph Montgolfier, paper-makers at Aimonay, in France, whose names are as distinguished in the development of their own branch of manufacture as in the history of aeronautics. It immediately struck these brothers, on reading Cavendish's Different Kinds of Air, that the air could be rendered navigable by enclosing a light gas within a covering of inconsiderable weight. Led by their avocation, they fixed upon paper as the most fitting material for the purpose, and first attemptedtomakeballoonsof paper tilled with inflammable air. Finding that these emptied them almost as soon as they were filled, uostet doning the paper as an unsuitable covering for the gas, they sought after another gas more suited to the paper. By a chain of false reasoning which need not here be detailed, they thought they found such in the gas which resulted from the combustion of slightly moistened straw and wool, which had, as they imagined, an upward tendency, not oidy from its being heated, but from its electrical properties , which caused it to be repelled from the ground. It is hardly necessary to say, that this so-calledMontgolti : no ad vantages for raising balloons other than that possessed by I air of any kind; in fact, the abundant smoke with which it Was mixed, by adding to its weight, rather detracted from its merits. At Avignon, in November 17S2. Stephen Mont ;■ ■llior first succeeded in causing a silk parallelopiped, of about 50 cubic feet, to rise to the roof of a room. Encouraged by this MS

;, the brothers made experiments on :i I a I e at Annonay with an equally happy result ; and finally, in June 1783, in the presence of the states of \ ivaraie, and of an immense multitude, they I B., .;") feet in diameter, to a height of 1500 feet. This last, nearly spherical in shape, was made of packeloth, covered with paper, and was heated by an iron ohoffer placed beneath it, in which 10 pounds of moist straw and wool were burned. The news of this extraordinary experiment soon reached Paris, where it produced a most lively impression. A commission was appointed l>y the Academy of Sciences to report upon it. Public curiosity , however, could not await the tardy decision of tins body, and accordingly a subscription was entered into to defray the expense of repeating the Annonay experiment. Such was the excitement that the subscription was filled in a few days, and the construction of the B. was intrusted to the brothers Robert, famous philosophical instrument-makers of the day, and to Professor Charles, a young but experienced physicist. As the detailed account of the Annonay ascent had not reached Paris, and as nothing was therefore known of the Montgolfier gas, Charles fixed upon hydrogen as the gas most likely to insure success. It was, however, a formidable undertaking to produce it in sullicient abundance for a B., as it was at that time only dealt with in small quantities in the lecture-room. By ingenuity and perseverance combined, he triumphed over this difficulty, and succeeded in filling, in the course of four days, a silk globe of 12 feet in diameter. This B. was transferred to the Champs de Mars, the largest open space in Paris, where, on the 27th of August 1783, it ascended in the presence of 300,000 spectators, half the population of the city. At the instance of the co n -ion already referred to, Stephen Montgolfier constructed a lirc- B., 72 feet high, and 41 feet in diameter. It ascended before the commission on the 12th of September 1783, but being held captive, it was much injured by a violent wind, which blew at the time, and after it descended it was finally broken up by heavy rains. Another was made of nearly the ane dimensions, which ascended on the lftth of the same month at Versailles, the king and royal family ' assisting ' at the spectacle. This ascent is worthy of note, from the fact that a sheep, a cock and a duck were placed in an ozier-basket attached to the lower part of the B., and that these first aerial voyagers reached the ground again in safety. The B. was now a. fail accompli, and it began to be seriously discussed whether it might not be serviceable as an air-ship for bearing men aloft as passengers. The solution of this question was first given by Pil&tre des Hosiers. In a V as the heated air-B. was called, 71 feet high, and 'IS feet in diameter, supporting at its base a gallery of wicker-work, he, in company with the .Marquis d'Arlandes, made the first aerial voyage, 21st November 1783. They remained in the air twenty-five minutes, and sailed across the Seine and over a considerable part of Paris. The year 1783, so fertile in the annals of ae'rostation, was destined not to pass away without witni an additional, and even more satisfactory triumph. On the 1st of December, Professor Charles, along with Robert, rose from the Tuilerics gardens with a hydrogen B. — then called a Chm made from the proceeds of a public subscription. This B. was made of alternately red and yellow gores of silk sewed together, and coated with caoutchouc varnish. It was covered with a net which supported the car, and was furnished with a valve, a barometer, and sand-ballast, and was, in fact, a complete aerial machine. It may be said that 6lt; the art of ae'rostation at once attained perfection in Charles's P., and no essential change or imprc incut has taken place since. In DOS BqUence of the danger attending the use of Eire-balloons, and the engrossing attention which they demand of the aeronaut, they have now entirely given way to the hydrogen or coal-gas balloons. Before they became obsolete, several remarkable voyages were made in them. The same Pilltre des Hosiers made 30 li in one of them, the longest voyage ever executed in a Montgolliere. Among the names of the fil I professional aeronauts, those of Lunardi, Blanchard, and Garnerin deserve special note. Lunardi was the first wdio made the ascent in Great Britain ; and Blanchard, along with the American Dr Ji crossed the English Channel from Dover to Calais in circumstances of almost unparalleled d January 7, 17S5. Garnerin first descended from a B. by a Parachute (q. v.), October 22, 17'.'7. It is much to be regretted that the first aeronaut, Pilfttre <les Rosiers, fell a victim to a blind devotion to his art. In order to outvie Blanchard he constructed a compound machine, consisting of a hydrogen B. above and a Montgolliere below, and started from Botdogne, accompanied by a young natural philosopher named Hoinain, on the morning 01 the 5th of June 1785. lie had not ascended many minutes, when, as it afterwards appeared, on attempting to open the valve of the hydrogen B. by the rope attached to it, he caused a rent of several yards in it, so that it emptied itself almost immediately, and fell on the Montgolliere beneath. The fire in the latter not being kindled, the whole machine fell with a frightful rapidity to the earth, and the ill-fated aeronauts perished on the spot whence they had risen. It is worthy of remark, that though several melancholy incidents of this kind are ou record, the number of casualties in the navigation of the air has been less in proportion than in the navigation of the sea. For 1500 aeronauts and 10,000 ascents, calculating approximately, only 15 lives have been lost, certainly a small prodi >i l inn considering dangers and inexperience. I n 1 794, during the wars of the Revolution, an aerostatic institution was formed at Meudon, near Paris, f< ir training a corps of ' aerostiers,' in order to observe the enemy by means of balloons. A balloon under the management of this corps was present at the battle of Fleiirus, near Charleroi, fought against the Austrians. During the siege of Paris. INTO 1S71, the P>. was extensively employed. Countless letters and several persons left the beleagured city iu balloons. There was, of course, no attempt made to come back in such a conveyance : carrier pigeons were the return messengers. Balloons have been enlisted iu In half of science. The first ascent for scientific objects was made at Hamburg, July 18, 1803, by Robertson and Lhoest. The results obtained, more particularly regarding the diminution of terrestrial magnetism, and the general feebleness of electrical and galvanic phenomena in the rarer portions of the atmosphere, ware considered of such importance by the French Insti- t ni •■, that another ascent was determined on; MM. Biot and Gay-Lussac were appointed to take tho management of the B. and of the physical experiments ; and they started, accordingly, on the 20th August 1804. As this aerial expedition was not altogether successful, a second was undertaken by Gay- Lussac alone, in the same year, in which he rose to a height of 23,000 feet. The observations of tho French savans did not confirm those made by Robertson, for after a series of experiments, as careful as their novel situation would admit, they found that no diminution was perceptible in the intensity of electrical phenomena in the upper air. Since

then, many scientific aerial voyages have been taken, among winch may be mentioned tint by Humboldt in America; those made by Mr Rnah, in c mpany with Mr Green as steersman, on behalf of the British Association, during 1 s 17 1849; that by MM. Barral and Bizu (1860) at Paris, J;> oily, the most remarkable ascents have made by MrGlaisher for meteorological observation. < in one occasion he ascended to a height of 7 1 miles the barometer standingatl inches. The B. contained 90,000 cubic feet of gas, and carried 60(1 bis. The uetric ami thermometric laws of the air may be ascertained by B. ascents. The nature of aerial currents, at present so imperfectly under might also be discovered by the sai The introduction of coal-gas, instead of hydrogen, by Mr i : ii, the most famous of English aeronauts, is the most important advance in aerostation since the earliest days of the art. His large coal-gas B., in 1888, bine Messrs Green, Holland, and Mason from Vauxhal! Gardens, London, to Weilburg, in the Grand Dnchyof Nassau, distant 500 miles, in 18 ho its. In the United States, aerostation has been prosecuted with great zeal. Mr J. Wise has more than once exploded his B., when high up in the air, to shew what he considers to be always the case, that the fragments with the net-work form in such circumstances a parachute, which moderates the rapidity of descent, and shields the aeronaut from i. During 1S59, the longest flight on record was made by Mr J. Wise, Mr La Mountain, and others, who, starting from St Louis with the intent i ' 1 1 1 of reaching New York, succeeded in following the course they had mapped out for themselves until they had crossed Lake Erie ; when they were caught in an adverse current of air, and forced to abandon their original design, after having travelled 1150 miles in less than '2i> hours. In September 1859, Mr La Mountain made a trip of 800 miles in 4 hours. Mr Lowe, another American aeronaut, constructed an immense B., which he, Called an aerial ship, the greatest circumference of which was .'1S7 feet, with a capacity to hold 700,000 cubic feet of gas, and a lifting-power of 22J tons, and furnished with many new appli: ivating, depressing, and directing the machine. In ls7.'i, Mr Wise undertook the construction of a bul hum to cross the Atlantic. He proposed to lay in -ii >res for 30 days.

ballot.c:
BA'LLOT (in French, ballotte) is a little ball used in the practice of secret voting, which is thence generally called ' voting by B.,' whether it be a ball or a ticket that is used. Votes may be taken by B. in various ways — e. g., the voter may deposit a ball in either of two boxes, so conjoined that no one shall be able to say into which he drops it ; or he may be presented with two balls — a white and a black — and so drop one of them into a box that it shall be unknown which he used. Tickets marked ' Yes,' ' No,' or with the names of candidates, will serve the purpose of balls in private voting. The Dikasts in Greece voted secretly by means of balls, stones, or shells, with marks. From this use of marked shells (Gr. ostrahon) in popular voting came the Greek i , or secret vote of the people, by which they drove into exile those who became obnoxious to them. Tabids or tickets were chiefly used by the Unmans. If the vote concerned a change in the law, the tickets were marked A'. EL, the initial letters of the words ' Uti Rogas,' • ing consent to the proposer's proposition; and A. hi" Antiquo,' e\] herence to the old law. If the vote concerned the election of candidates to a public office, then the tickets bore the names of the candidates. The system of secret voting in Rome was iixed by various laws, of which the Gabiniana Lex most closely resembles the modern project of vote by ballot. The system of vote by B. is much in use among moderns in private or social clubs, and in the i of officers and other acts of public or joint- stock companies. The propriety of employing it in private clubs has never been questioned, for to the harmony of these it is essential that the votes of a few should suffice to exclude an obnoxious person ; and looking to the personal and invidious na> the vote, it is equally essential to their hai that the voting should be secret. A candidal admission, who succeeds in the face of a few, though not a sufficient number of voters, could not but i rd those who voted against him as ened But if the voting be by B., all he can know, if the voters keep their uv, n counsel, is that soi are unfriendly. It is thus left open for him to associate on friendly terms with all 'hers — a condition of the success and continuance of such ations. But whether the system was to political and municipal voting, need to be in this country the subject of keen debate, at a time when it was in use in France, in several of the I States, and in the Australian cole We have said that the system prevailed in Greece, and on its fruit there — especially in the exercise of the ostracism — there have been various opinions. While some have considered that the Athenians, for instance, acted under cover of secrecy, frequently without a just sense of responsibility, there is the authority of MrGrote, in his History of Greece, on the other side, to the effect, that they exercised the right most beneficially. But if we have in Mr Grote an advocate of the B., in Gibbon we have an opponent of it. In his Decline and Fall of tlte Roman Empire, that philosopher dates the decline of the republic from the introduction of secret voting, which, he says, destroyed public confidence — in effect, broke up the ancient relations of patron and client, and caused a general demoralisation of the people. To come to modern times, we find the B. in use in the Venetian senate ; and that in Britain it was first demanded, not for the purpose of elections, but of votes in parliament. In Scotland, during the revulsions against the court in the reign of Charles II., the system was actually adopted in the legislature ; but it does not appear to have afforded voters in all cases the desired protection. No one would now dream of demanding its introduction in parliament, whose proceedings, according to popular opinion, cannot be too open and above board. On this point it may be mentioned that secret voting was the rule, for over five years (from 1840 — 1845), in the Chamber of Deputies in France, when it was abolished, as being productive of abuse. This, however, as we have said, bears on a use of the system that has now no advocates. Two illustrations remain of its use in elections. In the colonies of Melbourne and Sydney, the B. is said to have worked well, though it has been doubted whether its efficacy has been properly tested in these countries, in which there is so much individual independence, peculiar to new countries, thai who vote care little for concealment. In the United States, on the other hand, it is sand I neral opinion that the Bystem has proved inefficacious, tn the state of New York, where the B. was ad several years ago, there is now a party dem . as a cure for the evils introdui system. They say it has among the Americans opposed no effectual obstacle to coercion and intimidation from the majority, while th whom the arrangements for secrecy are int; flagrantly betray their trust, anil the voters on either side are, as a rule, well known to the public. 647

The advocates of the B. used to maintain that it would prevent bribery, intimidation, and undue influence. They regarded its reputed failure in America as being Inside the question as to its suitability for this country, becav ■ in America what the voter has to contend against is the pressure of the many, while with us hi I to resist coercion by individuals. The tenants, for iii they said, want security, through concealment, against the hiss of their farms, sin mid tln-y vote against the wishes of their landlord, They believed it would prevent bribery, through the uncertainty that the bribed party would vote as he promised. And as a candidate would not give bribe I, b he could not trust that he would get value for his money, so intimidation would not be attempted in the absence of any security that it would be of effect. To this it was answered, on the other side, that the case of America was in point, inasmuch as intimidation might arise here, as there, from a majority, and that the case of a shopkeeper and his patrons was that of many against one all over the world. If the li. failed to protect the unit against the crowd in one country, how could it succeed in another'; As to the undue influence of individuals over many — as of a landlord over his tenants — it could only he prevented providing the many, in all their public acts, contradict their secret votes. If tin; many acted publicly as if they agreed with the few, and privately voted against them, we should have had a state of things in which the profi public opinion would have been in antagonism with the public policy, supported by private votes — a state of things justly regarded as being impossible t" lie produced The influence of individuals, then, must remain — i. e., the secret voting would be of no use, since, short of lifelong hypocrisy, it must fail to be a protection. As to bribery, the opponents of the B. thought better of human nature than those who would purify it by machinery. 'Honour among thieves,' they said : 'he who takes a bribe, either has no principle left in him for which to vote contrary to his promise, or will be guided by his deceased sense of honour.' On the other view, they put it, you secure the vote of a rogue, through his playing the knave doubly, by the public in taking a bribe, and by the briber in not fulfilling his pledge. That men will be inclined to give and take bribes as formerly, despite the somewhat diminished security, they appeared not to doubt. An element in the controversy was the question — whether the franchise was to be regarded as a public trust, or a private power to be used at the individual's discretion. The opponents of the B. maintained the franchise to be a trust, on which view, certainly, it should be openly exercised. Its advocates, on the other view, held the object of the franchise to be the ascertainment of the conscientious opinions of the people. The fact is, the right partakes of both characters : it is a power of expressing opinion by the agent under a sense of responsibility. The B. gives greater security for independence of thought ; but the public vote is attended by the greater security for sense of responsibility. It used to be common to sprinkle pleas against the B. with high praise of the whole scheme of British pobtics, as open, manly, and candid, and with expressions of contempt for the B., as sneaking, and dissonant with that scheme. But the advocates of the B. were not unprepared with a ready and obvious retort to such arguments. Public feeUng was kept alive on this question by annual motions in parliament. From 1S35, its introduction was an open question with the Whigs. The Radicals, in ISd'.l, were greatly pleased to lind Lord John Russell expri I mself as being almost a convert to their views. The controversy was put an end to in .Inly 1872, when voting at parliamentary and municipal elections in Great Britain and Ireland was decreed to I"' by ballot.

balls.c: BALLS, Hollow. In military pyrotechny, many varieties of B. are made, differing in purpose from bomb-shells, but, like them, filled with ignitible composition. They are used to give light, to produce a dense smoke, or to diffuse a suffocating odour. Some of them, though called B., are not globular in shape. Light B. consist of a stretched over a skeleton-frame, and painted; the frame is tilled with a composition of saltpetre, sulphur , resin, and line. cd-oil, rammed down hard] and is provided with a fuse, the length of which determines the time that will elapse before tl m- ?osition ignites. These light B. weigh from 5 lbs. to 0 lbs. each, according to their size. They are intended to give out a brilliant light, which may reveal the operations of the enemy during night at a siege or in the held. Smoke-B. are made of several thicknesses of paper, shaped by I of a globular core or mould. They arc filled with gunpowder, saltpetre, powdered sea-coal, Swedish pitch, and tallow; and are calculated, after being tired oil', to send out a dense smoke for nearly half an hour, in order to blind or incommode the enemy. Stink-B. are filled with a composition which, when ignited, diffuses an odour almost intolerable. Some of the contrivances of Captain Norton and other inventors at the present day, noticed under Asphyxiants, are extensions of the same principle as these inflammable balls. It may here be added, that most of these projectiles, especially light J!, and smokc-B., arc tired from mortars, rather than from guns.

bally.c: BA'LLY, BAB, a Celtic word or prefix, signifying 'town' or 'dwelling,' enters into the composition of hundred:; of names of places in Ireland and Scotland It is allied (see letter B) to Or. polis, city, and to the Lat., Ital., and Span, villa.

ballycastle.c: BALLYCA'STLE, a small seaport town in the north of Antrim county, Ireland, in an open bay opposite Rathlin Isle, S8 miles north of Belfast, and 5 miles south- west. of Fairhead. It lies at the base of Knocklayd Mountain, 1635 feet high ; and the marine and mountain scenery around is very romantic . B. consists of an upper and lower town, a quarter of a mile apart. Its harbour and pier en t £150,000, but the former is now filled with sand. Coal was dug here at least 500 years ago. Linen manufacture and salmon-lishcry are carried on here. Near B. are the Bonnamargy Abbey ruins. There is a singular iissure, called the 'Gray .Man's Path,' in the face of a greenstone precipice near li. on the way to Fairhead. Pop. (1S71) 1626. BALEYMEXA, a small inland town in the centre of Antrim county, Ireland, in a plain, on the right bank of the Braid, 2 miles above its junction with the Maine, and .'l.'i miles north-nortli-wesl of Belfast. It lies in a densely peopled and well-cultivated district, the inhabitants uniting the pursuit of agriculture with the manufacture 01 linen. B. is one of the greatest linen and flax markets in Ireland, and its vicinity is covered with extensive bleach-fields. Pop. (1871) 7G2S.

ballyshannon.c:
BALLYSHA'NNON, a small seaport town in the south of Donegal county, Ireland, the chief town of the county, though not the capital. It is situated at the mouth of the river Erne, on a

email inlet running off from Donegal Bay, and 1 'ii miles north-west of Dublin. A bridge of 14 crosses the Erne here. The Erne dl» b more water than any other Irish river except the Shannon, and falls 140 feet over a rugged bed in the last 9 miles oi its course; 400 yards below the bridge at B. the river falls in a cataract 1G feet high at low water, and 450 feet wide, over a limestone ledge of rock. The chief streets of ];. are verj steep. There is a valuable salmon- flshery on the river. The export trade is small, in consequence of the existence of a bar at the mouth oi the harbour and the prevalence of west winds. Pop. (1871) 2909. 13AT,M (MdUaa officinalis), an erect, branching, perennial, herbaceous plant, of the natural order Zabiaice, a native of the south of Europe, naturalised In a few places ill England. It has ovate crenate Balm {Melissa officinalis). leaves, and axillary half-whnrls of white flowers on one side of the stem. The whole plant has an i.l>' lemon-like smell, on account of which it is frequently cultivated in gardens. The stilus and leaves are used in medicine as a gentle aromatic, stimulant, and tonic. 15. is also employed for making an agreeable and somewhat exhilarating beverage railed B. Wine. B. was formerly in much in ii i repute than now for its medicinal virtues. Its qualities depend on an essential oil of a pale yellow colour, called Oil of Balm. For medical use, the herb should be cut before the appearance of the flowers, which begin to expand in .Inly. It is nearly inodorous when dried. Tin' baste is somewhat austere, and slightly aromatic B. scarcely produces any remedial operation Upon the system. The quantity of oil which it contains is mil more than sufficient to communicate a pleasant flavour to the iiifusum, which forms an excellent drink in febrile complaints, and when taken warm, tends to [promote the operation of diaphoretic medicines. — A variety of the common Cat mint (Nepeta cataria), with a smell like that of B., is often mistaken for it. — MOLDAVIAN B. (Vracooj)halaui Muldaciaun) is a native of the country from which it derives its name, and of Siberia, &c. ; an annual plant, having, when a smell like that of B., but less pleasant. It is much used in Germany for flavouring dishes. — Bastard l>- (.!/■ a native of the south of England and of many parts ": Europe, is a very beautiful plant, which when dried has a delightful fragrance, and retains it long. All I arc of the natural order Labiakc.

balmofgilead.c: BALM OF GI'LEAD. See Balsam of Gilead.

balmoralcastle.c: BALMO'RAL CASTLE, the autumnal residence of Her Majesty Queen Victoria, is situated in a beautiful dell in Braemar (the south-west district of Aberdeenshire), on a natural platform that gently down from the base of Craigan-gowan I margin of the river Dee in front; and about 48 miles west of the city of Aberdeen. The i commands a magnificent prospect on all side I 1848, Prince Albert purchased the reversion of a 38 years' lease from the representatives of Sir 1 1 Gordon, who had held it under the Earl oi and in 1852 he acquired the fee-simple of the • from the Fife trustees for a sum of £32,000. The old castle not being sufficiently commodious for the royal family, Prince Albert erected a new one at his own expense, in what is called the Scot, style of architecture. The castle consists i separate blocks of building, united by wings and a massive tower 35 feet square, rising to the I of 80 feet, surmounted by a turret 20 At a distance, the castle, which is built of granite, has a strung and imposing appearance, looking almost as if it had been hewn out of one huge rock of that material. Great improvements have been made, chiefly those projected by the late Prince Albert in the approach', to the co; i Tin' estate now includes Birkhall, Knoel ruins, Loch Miiick, and 'dark Lochnagar,' celebrated by Byron (which is about seven miles south- v, B. C), and contains about 10,000 acres, in addition to 30,000 acres of hill-ground, which hai b verted into a deer-fo

balnaves.c:
BA'LNAVES, HENRY, of Halhill, an eminent lay- reformer of the 10th c. Born at Kirkcaldy in shire of poor parents, who, however, contrived to give him a university education at St Andn ws, In' went to the continent, and entered a free school at Cologne, where he greatly improved his scholarship, ami received instruction in the principles of the new faith which Luther had just promulgated. <>n his return to Scotland, he studied law, and for some time as a procurator at St Andrews. In 1538, James V. made him a senator of the ( of Justice; and on Arran being appointed to the regency, B. was made secretary of state. In 1643, he was imprisoned on account of his Protestant! appears to have been liberated in the following year. He new appears to have made bin on the Protestant side; and it is asserted that he was privy to the conspiracy formed for the mm Cardinal Beaton, and that he acted for tl spirators at the English court. In 1547, 1"' took n in ' m the Castle "i si Andrews, ami >■ a traitor and excommunicated. When the castle was captured by the French, B., with Knox and < w. le sent to Rouen as prisoners of war. W I prison here, B. wrote a treatise on Justification, to which Knox a Med marginal not'-', and prefixed a dedication, and which was afterwards published with the title of Tit < !\u!h. When Maiy of Guise was raised to the n in 1554, B.'s forfeiture was rescinded, and he returned to Scotland, and took an active part on ih ide of the Lords of the I on, by whom he was appointed one of the commissi.. ners

who Battled the treaty of Berwick in 1559 — 1560, which established by law the reformed religion in Scotland. In 15ti.'>, B. was Dominated a commute revise The Book qf DitcApline. He after- acted for the Regent Murray in the inquiry into the charges against Mary for the murder of Damley. lie died in 1579; one account says 1570. Both Knox and Melville had a high opinion of him alike for his piety, wisdom, and learning. B VLSAM, a name formerly comprehensive of many resinous substances and oils, to which important medicinal virtues were ascribed, as well &S of medicines compounded of resins and oils. When the term B. is now used without addition, the balsams of Peru and Tolu are generally intended. — These two balsams are very similar in all their more important properties, and are both produced by trees of the genus Myroaparmum (or Myroxylon), of the natural order Leyitmiiioso; sub-order Papilionoeeo, natives of the tropical parts of America. M. perui- fi rum, which is called theQninquino, a beautiful tree, common from Peru to Mexico, is generally rej as the species which produces the B. of Peru; ami M. In! nil', rum. a very similar species, found on the mountains of Tolu, the banks of the Magdalena, &c., as that which produces the B. of Tolu; but it is doubtful if the difference is not at least as much owing to the modes of procuring and preserving the B. ; and other species of the same genus (.'/. puno totem and M. pubescens) are supposed also to yield it. 11. of Peru appears in two forms, known as White n. of Peru and Black B. qf Peru ; the former of which has been said to be obtained from the pods, and the latter from incisions in the trunk of the tree ; but it has also been stated that the white B. flows from the trunk, and that the black B. is obtained by distilling down the wood after the manner Of tar burning, or by boiling with water. The actual evidence is insufficient to determine these points with certainty, and it is not improbable that different methods may be employed. White B. of Peru is at first of the consistence of recent honey, and of a light yellow colour ; the 1 Jack B. is of a reddish or blackish brown colour, and of the consistence of treacle. B. of Tolu, until recently, appeared in commerce day and friable, but is now generally soft and tenacious when first imported, becoming hard by age. Both balsams have a very fragrant odour. They are used in confectionary, to impart a flavour like that of vauillc; also in perfumery, and for pastilles, &c. In medicine, they are administered as gentle stimulants and tonics, and particularly in chronic bronchial affections. Tolu lozenges are a popular and pleasant remedy for troublesome coughs. These balsams are also used for cleansing ulcers. — They contain Cinnamic Acid, and a peculiar oily substance which has been called Cinnameine, and is also known as Oil of B. of Peru. The name White B. qf Peru is sometimes given to a balsamic substance which flows from the Liquidambar styracifiua. See Liqutdaaibai:.

balotra.c: BALO'TRA, a town of India, in the R.ajpoot state of Joudpore, 59 miles south-west of the city of Joudpore. It is situated on the right bank of the river Looueo. Being on the high-road from Joud- jiiire to Dwarka, a celebrated place of pilgi-image iu the west of Guzerat, it is a great resort of pilgrims, with whom its bazaar is often crowded. Many of tlio inhabitants of the town subsist by providing for their wants. The town is supplied with good water from 125 wells, lined with masonry. Pop. 7275.

balsam.c: BALSAM, or BALM OF GILEAD, is a liquid resinous substance, which has long enjoyed a very high reputation in the East, being prized not only for its fragrance, but also for the medicinal virtues which it is supposed to possess. It is the subject of several allusions in the Old Testament, which strongly indicate the prevalent opinion of its preciousness ; and is celebrated by Strabo, Pliny, Diodorus Siculus, and other ancient writers, almost as a cure for every disease. It is still somewhat doubtful what tree furnishes it, but it is generally believed to be a species of Balsamodendron (q. v.) — a small tree growing in Arabia and Abyssinia, and known as B. Gileadense. The finest balsam, called WO Opobalsam or Balm of Mecca, is obtained by incisions , is at first turbid and white, but finally becomes of a golden yellow colour, and of a consistence like honey. Inferior kinds are obtained by boiling the fruit and the wood. B. of Gilead is irritating when applied to the skin, and is believed to resemble B. 01 Capaiva in its effects upon the human system. Balsamodendron Opobalsamum, a species very nearly allied to B. Gileadense, is sometimes said to furnish this balsam. Other substances, sometimes designated bal and possessing a somewhat similar fragrance, are produced by different species of Aim/ridacca (q. v.). Among them is one called American Balm of Gilead, the produce of a tree called /ci'ra Corona. — Balsamic substances are furnished also by a number of sp< of Clusiacea; — Balsam of Umiri, a fragrant yellow fluid, by Ilumirium jUirinvinhnii, a South American tree, of the natural order Humiriacece.- CANADIAN BaI 3AM is a kind of turpentine obtained from the Balm of Gilead Fir (Abies balsa/mea); Hungarian Balsam, from the Mugho or Mountain Pine {Pimm Pumilio or Mughus); and CARPATHIAN Balsam, from the Stone Pine (Piniis pinca). See Fin and Pine. — Balsam of Copatva is the produce of different species of Copaifcra. See CoPATVA.

BALSAM is also the common name of a natural order of succulent herbaceous plants, BaUaminea or B'tlsaminaeece of botanists, of which the beautiful B. (Impatiens bahamina or Balsamina horteneis), Balsam [Impatiens Noli-me-tangcrc). a, top of stem with leaves ami flowers ; '<, ripe fruit unopened ; c, ripe fruit, elastically opening. so much cultivated in gardens and green-houses, is a familiar example. Upwards of one hundred species are known, natives chiefly of damp bushy places in the East Indies, and many of them plants of great beauty. They are almost all annuals, and have generally white or red flowers. This natural order is very closely allied to Geraniaceie (see Geranium) and Oxalideoz (q. v.), wood-sorrel, &c, but is distinguished from both by the extreme irregularity of the flowers, and from the former also, by the beakless fruit, which is a five-celled capsule, bursting by five elastic valves. The leaves are simple and without stipules, the flowers generally axillary. — The common B. is a native of the

i I Indies and Japan. Many fine varieties have resulted from careful cultivation. It has an w, succulent stem, usually about 1 — - feet high, suit in favourable circumstance* will attain a gj size. It often appears with flowers parti ill*, a. but still capable of producing seed. In Britain, the I usually sown on a alight hotbed, and the plant is often kept in the green-house; although even in Scotland it may be made an ornament of a sheltered border. It is one of the flowa qucntly to be seen in cottage-windows. A vulnerary was formerly prepared from it, whence it has its One species of B. (Impatient Nob I called Yellow B. or Touch-me-not, is a native oi Europe, and a doubtful native of Britain. It has yellow flowers, and one of the petals prolonged into a spur, its ripe capsules burst on the slightest touch. This and two other species are natives of North America.

balsamodendron.c: BALSAMODE'NDRON (Gr. balsam-tree), a genus of small trees or bushes of the natural order A myridaeea (q. v.), having small green axillary I i, small dry oval fruits, and small pinnated leaves with 3 or 5 leaflets. Some of them are spiny : they generally exhibit a scrubby appearance, and have little foliage. They are remarkable for the balsamic substances obtained from their wood ami fruit — as Balsam of Gilead (q. v.), Myrrh [q. v.), Bdellium (q. v.), and Oriental Elemi (q. v.). The red resinous wood of B. Kalof is a common article of sale in -Egypt ; and a species called Schnee is much cultivated in Afghanistan for its aromatic and stimulant properties. All the known species are natives of the East Indies, Arabia, and the east of Africa, except that which yields African bdellium, which is found in Senegal.

balsamopsulphur.c: BA'LSAM OP SU'LPHUR is a mixture employed for medicinal purposes, and considered of service when applied to foul ulcers. It is prepared by dissolving 1 part of flowers of sulphur in 8 parts 01 olive oil, which yield a dark, reddish brown, thickish substance, with a very unpleasant odour.

baltea.c: BA'LTA, a well-built and thriving town on the Kodema, an affluent of the Bug, in the government , of Podolia, Russian Poland. Pop. (1867) 1 1,528.

balticprovinces.c: BA'LTIC PRO'VINCES (in Russia). This term, in a wider sense, comprehends the five Russian governments bordering on the Baltic — viz., Court .iii.l, Livonia, Esthoma, Petersburg, and Finland; in a restricted sense, it often designates the first three. The B. P. once belonged to Sweden, except Courland, which was a dependency of Poland They came into the possession of Russia partly in the be inning of the 18th c., through the conquests of Peter the Great, partly under Alexander in 1S09. They have still very various constitutions, though the usual ' government ' machinery has been introduced , and every effort is made completely to Russianise them. The five governments have an area of about 200,000 square miles, with a population in 1867, of 4,902,543, including St Petersburg.

balticsea.c: BA'LTIC SEA, is the great gulf or shut sea bordered by Denmark, Germany, Russia, and Sweden, and communicating with the Kattegat and North Sea, by the Sound and the Great and Little Belts. Its length is from S50 to 900 miles ; breadth, from 100 to 200; and area, including the Gulfs of Bothnia and Fiidand, about 160,000 square miles. Its depth is on an average IS— 20 fathoms, in many places not half so much, seldom moxi 40 — 50, and never exceeding 167. Its shallowness an.l narrowness, the flat coasts of Prussia on the one side and the rooky coasts of Sweden on the other, and above all the numerous and sudden changes of wind accompanied by violent storms, make the navigation of the Baltic very dangerous. The group of tin- Aland Islands divide the south part of tl from the north part or Gulf of Bothnia (q. v.). The Gulf of Finland (q. v.), branching off eastwards into Russia, m Estl ia. A third gulf is that of Riga or Livonia. The Kuri-i other Hails (q. v.) are not gulfs, but fresh-water lakes at the mouths of rivers. The water of the I older and clearer thr.n that of the ocean. It contains only a tilth of the salt of the Atlantic, and ice hinders its navigation from three to five months yearly. Tides, as in all inland seas, are little perceptible— at Copenhagen, about a foot ; yet the water rises and falls at I though from other causes, chiefly from the \ quantity of water in the rivers at different seasons. Upwards of 'Joli nvers flow into this sea. Tl. from Germany are the Trave, Waruow. Oder, I', a ant.', Vistula, 1'lVL" !. and Nielneli ; from 1. the Windau, Diina, Narva, Neva, and Ulea ; and from Sweden, Tornea, I.ulea, l'itea, Umca, Anger- man, Dal, the water of Lake Maeler, and that of Wetter and other lakes through the river Motala. The basin of the Baltic occupies at least 888,710 square miles, or about one-fourth of all Europe; and only about a fourth of the boundary of the basin is mountainous. The principal islands are Zealand, Fiinen, Bornholm, Samsiie, Moen, Langeland, and Laaland, belonging to Denmark ; the Swedish islands Gottland, Gland, and Hvecn (in the Sound) ; the Aland Islands, Dago, and OescL, belonging to Russia; and Rugcn, to Prussia. The number of vessels that pass the Sound to or from the Baltic annually is very large. See Souxd Dues. Timber, sides, tallow, and grain, are the chief c from the countries bordering on the Baltic. The Eider or Schleswig-Holstein Canal, connecting the Baltic near Kiel with the North Sea at Tonningen, facilitates the grain trade in mild winters. The two seas are also connected by the Gotha Canal, which joins the lakes of South Sweden. The most important harbours in the Baltic are : in Denmark, Copenhagen and Klonsburg : in < ■ rinany, Schleswig, Kiel, Travemtinde (Lubcek), Wismar, K Stralsund, Stettin, Swinemtinde, Da ESbing, sberg, Pillau, and Memcl ; in Russia, Riga, Revel, Narwa, Kronstadt, and Sveaborg ; and in Sweden, Stockholm, Karlskrona, and Ystad.— The shores of the Baltic in Prussia and Courland have been long noted for the amber cast ashore by the waves in stormy weather. Another important phenomenon connected with the Baltic, is an slow vertical movement of its coasts, downward* in the south of Sweden, but further north upi being there supposed to be at the rate of thin iu a century. See Lyell's Principles of Geoloyt/. — The Germanic nations call tii I astern Sea ; the name Baltie is derived by Dr Latham, from an island I '.alt ia. mentioned by 1 'liny, and which Di Latham i aiders to be Zealand.

baltimore.c:
HA LTIMORE, a city, port of entry, and justice of Baltimore county, Maryland, I'. s., in Lit. 39" 17 S.t and long. 76 36' W. It stands round a small bay which runs back from the left side of the PatapsCO, about 12 miles from its entrance into Chesap.'do' Bay, and about 200 miles, by a ship's open Atlantic. The city III le 1 so late as 17-9. The a of its prosperity is to be found in the sue lultsoj i I in mi >. there were 26,51 1 inhabitants; in 1810,46,455; iii 1820, 62,738; in 1830, 80,620; in 1840, 102,613; in I860, 160,064 ; in Is.-,:;, about 195,000; and in 1S70 there were 267,354, Besides ita safe and convenient communication with the sea, B. is connected by railway with 651

Philadelphia, Washington, Winchester, Annapolis, Cumberland, York, Lancaster, and Harrisburg. Prom ea I to (rest, tl ity is about 4.\ miles |..,,- ; and from ill, to south, about 3J broad, and covi : about 10,000 acres. li is divided into two Qearly equal parts by 'Jones's Falls,' a rapid Btream which, though troublesome from its Hoods, and expensive from its bridges, at once affords immense water- power, and supplies an abundance of pure water fur aomesi ic ai Imports in 1868 amounted to 12,930,7:;:; dollars; and the exports to 13,857,391. In the same year, •_".l!l vessels, of 115,140 tonnage, entered the port, and 595, of 21 1,250, cleared it. There are 25 papers, 8 of which are dailies. Among the commemorative structures which have gained for B. the name of the 'Monumi stal City,' the most interesting is an elegant obelisk, which was erected in 1815 to the memory of tlio.se who had fallen the year before in defending the town against an attack of the British. As In' expected in the wealthiest city of Roman Catholic- Maryland, the Roman Catholic cathedral takes the lead among the ecclesiastical edifices of B. It is a massive building of granite, being 190 feet long, 177 broad, and to the top of the cross, 127 high : and besides one of the largest organs in the United States, it contains two beautiful paintings, presented respectively by Louis XVI. and Charles X. of France. In B., however, the Roman Catholics are now vastly outnumbered by oth -r denominations, hiving only 20 churches out of 161.

baltimorebird.c: BA'LTIMORE-BIRD, or BALTIMORE ORIOLE (Tclerua Baltimorii), a very beautiful American bird, found in all parts of the United Baltimore-Bird. States, and as far north as 55° N. lat., but migrating to tropical or subtropical regions in winter. The genus to which it belongs is usually referred to the natural family of SiurnidoB (see Starling). The B.-B. is in size somewhat less than a common starling ; the bill conical, very acute, and a little curved ; the plumage brilliant, particularly in the adidt males, glossy black finely contrasting with bright orange and vermilion ; the tail longish, rounded, and slightly forked. The bird is remarkably active and lively; its song extremely agreeable. Its nest is a curious and interesting structure — a pendulous cylindrical pouch of six or seven inches long, usually suspended from two twigs at the 652 extremity of a lofty drooping branch; the materials, which vary according to circumstances, being woven together with great nicety. It is sometimes sewed through and through with long horse-hairs. Thread, which may happen to l»- iiie.-iehing, is very liable to be appropriated to the purpose of nest-building. The nests of other species of Icterus are also pensile. Several are natives of North America, and others of South America. They are quite distinct from the true Orioles (q. v.).

baltschik.c: BALTSCHI'K, or BALI UI'IC, a town of Europe,,,, Turkey, 18 miles north-east of Varna, noteworthy in consequence of being in the vicinity of the ruins of Tomi, to which place Ovid was exiled.

baluster.c: BA'LUSTER, popularly, banister or ballaster, (Ital. balaustro ; Fr. Iialustre), the name given to the small shafts or pillars set in a line at short Balusters. equal distances, and supporting a cornice or coping. These miniature pillars have generally either a pear-shaped swelling at the lower end, or consist of two pear-shaped pieces, placed above each other, a ring of mouldings being set between them. This makes the profile resemble an ancient bow or Balista (q. v.), from which some derive the name; others derive it from Lat. palus, Eng. pole or pale.

balustrade.c: BALUSTRADE, a range of balusters, together with the cornice or coping which they support The B. is often used as a parapet for bridges, the Balustrade. roofs of large edifices, &c., or as a mere termination to the structure. It is also used to enclose stairs, altars, balconies, &c. Balustrades are made of stone, metal, or wood.

balzac.c:
BALZAC, Jean Louis Gunz de, born at AngoulOme in 1594. In his youth he was secretary to Cardinal la Valctte at Rome, where he cultivated his taste for elegant composition, and on his return to Paris devoted himself to the refinement of his native language. His efforts in this direction have given him a permanent place in the literature of his country; and though his writings do not possess much intrinsic worth, they heralded the splendid phalanx of genius which adorned the subsequent age of Louis XIV. He was a favourite of Cardinal Richelieu, a member of the French Academy, a councillor of state, and historiographer. His violent literary disputes with Father Goula, caused him to leave Paris and retire to his hereditary property of Balzac, where he died on the

18th February 1655. A collection "f the wori appeared in Paris, edited by L'AbbS Cassaigne (2 role. Par. 1665; •>' vols, Amst L684). I his works, his Leltret (3 vols. Par. 1800) have been most generally admired, and arc still read. A selection from his writings was arranged by Malitourne (2 vols. Par. 1822). Compare Moreau de Ces de B. (Par. 1807).

BALZAC, Honors de, one of the best of the modern French novelist/, was born on the 20th May 1799, at Tours, where his father held a civil At the age of twelve, he entered the college df Venddme, but finished his studies at the Pension Lepitre, in Paris. His father, who had been imposed by the loss of his situation, then placed with a notary, to whom he acted as clerk. 'II:: occupation proving intolerably irksome, B. soon after began bis literary career, and wrote about 30 volumes, under the names, St Aubin, M. de Veillergrc, St Abne, &c. Ho received some I nee in writing these novels, which were, however, so unsuccessful, that he lived in the t poverty. In the year 1826, he en into partnership with the printer Barbier, and published various works; but the speculation turned out so ill, that he fell into debt, and returned once more to book-making. His perseverance was admirable. Although long utterly unsuccessful, ho continued to write on until at last he opened a path for himself by his novel Les Derniers Ohouans, ou la Bretagnt en 1800 (Par. 1829). In this book be abandoned for the first time the manner of Pigault and I.ebrun, which he had hitherto adopted. Among bis best works are the iogit du IWari \i (2 vol 1. Par. 1831), 8dn d< Ar I.- /'. '■■' (5vols. 1831), S&nesde la Vie de Pro- (] Vie Parisiennc (1832), Le Midtcin '/> Campagne, Le Pere Qoriot, La Peau de Chagrin, J." Recherche de VAbsolu, whh-h were all received with much favour by the public. Of all bis novels, two only can lay claim to anything like artistic completeness. They are the Sietoire Intel- 'le de Louis Lambert, and Eugeni Qra ■' His other works suffer more or less from unnaturalness , difroseness, and the wantof a solid knowled ■ of the world, although there is a richness of description in portraying individual features of character, as drawn directly from the heart, not to be denied. B. exercises immense power over the female part of his readers. In his Contes ])i;J,i/ii/m .',..,///./(<- <".< Ahhuies de Touraiiir, el mis an lumiere par le Sieur de Balzac pour Vesbattement de Pantagruelistes el non aultres (2 vols. Par. 18.'i3), he follows exactly in the footsteps of Rabelais. Success made B. conceitedly ambitious. He thought i f equal to the most distinguished authors of all time, and represented the aim of his literary activity to be, to give a complete picture of human lit'.' in all its varied phases. As a dramatic author he decidedly failed. In the year lS.">n, he was seized with hypertrophy of the heart, of which ho died on the I Ml. d August. Almost the whole literary world of Taris were present at his funeral. liAMBA'KRA, one of the states of .v Western Africa, lying, so far .as has been I 1, between lat. IT and 14° X., long. 15 E. and .ri W., and occupying both sides of the Joliba or Niger, which flows through its centre from west to north-east. The principal towns of B. Stand on the banks of this river. The mountains in which the Ni er has its Bource divide it on the S. from Guinea; the Sahara desert bounds it on the X.; on the W., Senegambia; and on the 1.'.. some of its sister-states. In its general aspect, the country is said to bear a considerable I lance to the agricultural districts of England ; but in the west there are low chains of granite hills, forming continuations of the highlands from which the Niger springs. The climate in some parts is intensely hot; in others, it is more temperate, but it is generally healthy. The rainy season lasts from June to November. The land is well v. and fertile. Double crops of corn, rice, maize, yams, &c, are raised annually without much labour. The butter-tree, cotton-tree, oil-palm, baobab, and date, are among the most important growths. The manufacturing u important; the women making a soft coarse cloth, much esteemed for its beautiful blue colour, and the men articles in gold, aan, and ivory, in which a pretty exl le is carried on. The inhabitants , chii fl ' id to be superior r neighbours in intelligence, and to be much sought after as warriors by the petty chiefs around them, who are at constant war with each other. They generally lend their assistance on condition of a certain payment. The up] > Mohammedanism, but the lower are pagans. The introduction of the former religion has had a1 one good i lied the native' dialect with a written speech through the use of Arabic letters. The chief domestic animals are b cattle, goats, sheep, and line horses. The wild animals are lions, leopards, elephants, woh &c. ; and venomous reptiles, of which the i. are much afraid. Crocodiles are numerous in the rivers, which also abound with fish. The principal towns are Sego, Sansandintr, Yamiua, and Bammakn, which are all populous. The country has a nominal monarch, but it is in reality ruled by several chiefs.

bamberg.c: BA'MBEBG, a city of Bavaria, in th Upper Francouia, beautifully situated on the of the Eegnitz, not far from its confluence with the Main, and in the midst of v rchards, and irdens. B., which has considerably de in importance since the Reformation, is a city of considerable antiquity, l:a\ ing originated, it is said, with a colony of Saxons who sailed here in S(M. The most noteworthy of its public build • the cathedral, a magnificent edifice in the Byzantine style, foimded by the Emperor Henry II. in I aud restored after lire in 1110. It contains, among other monuments, the elaborately carved tomb of the founder and his empress, C'unigunda. Attached to the cathedral is a library, with valuable I and manuscripts, aud what is represen be the prayer-book of Henry IL There are several either line ecclesiastical structures of early date, and the old palace of the former prince-bishops of Bam- The ruins of the castle of Altcnburg, originally the seat of the Counts of Babcnberg, au i scene of many important historical events, stand on an eminence about a mile and a half from the town. The educational institutions of B. arc numerous. Top. (1S71) 25,748, chiefly enga :- 1 in the manu- factur b which is famous throughout Germany , porcelain, jewellery, gloves, musical instruments , &c. A large export trade in liquorice and garden-seeds is carried on.

bambino.c:
BAMBI'NO, a term in art descriptive of the swaddled figure of the infant Saviour, which, surrounded by a halo, and watched over by angels, occasionally forms the subject of altar-pieces in Roman I catholic churches. XI i !'•.. in irch of the Ara Cceli at Borne, is held in veneration for its supposed miraculous power of curing the sick. It is carved in wood, painted, and richly decorated with jewels and precious stones. . irving is attributed to a Franciscan pilgrim, out of a tree that grew on Mount Olivet, and the an

painting to Bt Lake. The festival of the B., which at the Epiphany, is attended by great minii i of country people, and tho 15. is said to draw mora hi tlic shape of fees than the most successful medical practitioner in Borne,

bambocciades.c: BAMBO'CCIADES, in painting, are grot. ■ from common or low life — such as country- fain, penny-weddings, boon merry-making. The name is derived from I'ctcr van Laar, a painter, who, on account of his penonal deformity, was surnamed Bamboccio (Cripple) ; but he was not tho first painter of such scenes. BAMBOO' [Bambtua), a genua of passes, of whk-h most of the species attain a great size, many of them 20 or ."ill feet, some 70 or LOO feet in '• The species are numerous, and are found in tropical and subtropical regions, both of the eastern and i i vs. They are of great importance to the inhabitants of the countries iu which they grow. All of them have a jointed subten root-stock (rhizome), which throws up 10 — 100 stems. These are generally straight and erect ; although one large species (B. ayreslh), common in dry mountainous situations in the south-east of Asia, has croc iked, and sometimes creeping stems. The stems grow to their full height unbranched, but afterwards throw out straight horizontal branches, especially in their upper parts, forming a dense thicket; and many of them being strongly armed with spines, the planted for di fence, presenting a formidable barrier, ■'ar troops. Someof the smaller kinds are often planted as hedges. The stems are jointed Bamboo. like those of other grasses, very hard, but light and elastic, hollow, containing only a light spongy pith) except at the joints or nodes, where tin \ by strong partitions. They are. therefore, I converted into water-vessels of various sorts ; and when the partitions are removed, they are used as pipes for conveying water. They are also much employed for house-building, for bridges, and for many other purposes to which wood is usually applied. The smaller stems are converted into walking-sticks, and are imported into Europe Under the name of B. Cane, both for that purpose and to be employed in light wicker-work. Some of the ie now to the height only of a few feet; and almost all of them are slender in proportion to their height, although B. Gxadua, a native of Now Granada and Quito, has a trunk 16 inches in diameter . The stems of dillerent species vary also very much in the thickness of the woody part, and so in their adaptation to different purposes. The externa] covering of the stem is, in all the species, remarkably siliciotis ; the stem of /;. tabaca ria is so hard that it strikes lire when the hatchet is applied. This species is a native of Ajnboyna and Java; its slender stem J, and used for the stalks of ■ -pipes. The leaves of some kinds are n for thatch, and the CM] hats of thl I the external membrane of the stems of some, they make paper. From the knots of the 1'.. there exudes i: nine juice, which dries upon in the atmosphere, and which the Greeks ''aided Indian Honey. It is also i ■ , slieer ; but this name more properly belongs to a phosphorescent substance, containin I lime, and possessing remarkable properties, v. Inch forms in the joints of some S] oi I'.., and of BB growing in dry situations. See Taba- -The young shoots of some kinds of Ii. are like asparagus, or are pickled in vinegar. Those of B. Tulda, a common Bengalees used fur these purposes when about 2 Ie, | The seeds of some species are used as rice, and for ig a kind of beer. Bamboos are ; ■ very rapid growth, and they are often found in arid situations, which would otherwise be destitute of vegetation. It is not improbable that they may yet be employed, where they do not naturally abound, to render districts productive which are now little else than deserts, iii climates like those of Arabia, the north of Africa, and Australia; and the quality of the grain of dillerent species seems to 6j more attention than it has ever received. The common in the West Indies (/!. vulgaris) is ed to have been introdl d from the I Indies. A few species are found in the II inula an altitude of 12,000 feet, ami a dwarf species from :ioii has been successfully tried in the air in England. BAM BOU'K, a country of Senegambia, Western Africa, lying iii the angle formed by the 8 cine river, in N. lat. 12 W — 14° and YV. long. HI — 12' 30'. lis extent, however, has not been accurately a . but is roughly esti- at 140 miles iii length, and from .so to 100 in breadth. It is populated by Mandingoes, who are ferocious and cruel in the extreme. The climate is sultry and unhealthy, especially during the rainy i. Low ranges of mountains cover the greatest portion of the surface of B. The intervening valleys, which are subject to inundations, are h ible for their fertility. Trees common to rn Africa here attain enormous proportions. Vast herds of wild oxen roam the hills, and the most formidable wild annuals of Africa arc found in the forests and rivers. B., however, is chiefly : able for its rich gold-mines, the produce of which the natives exchange for salt, cotton, and other manufactured goods. Its inhabitants are professedly Mohammedans, but they cling to many of the ] lagan superstitions. B. was, four centuries ago, in the possession of the Portuguese, but they r to have been soon driven out.

bambrugh.c:
BA'MBR< >UGH, or B.VMBOROUGH CASTLE, one of the oldest castles in Britain, on the coast of Northumberland, IG miles south-east of Berwick, and crowning a basalt rock, rising 150 feet above the sea, and accessible only on the south-east. In this rock is a draw-well, 145 feet deep, sunk through the basalt into the sandstone below. B. Castle was founded in 1070. It was forfeited by the Pin Ms in 1715, but afterwards purchased by a scion of the same house. Lord Crewe, Bishop of Durham, who bequeathed the castle aud estate for

charitable purposes. In 1830, the income of the charity was upwards of A'8000. Connected with tin- castle is a market for the sale of provisions and groceries to the poor at prime cost ; a dispensary for gratis advice and distribution of medicines to the sick; funds fur lodging, clothing, and educating ; the children of the poor gratis; an extensive . , open to all living within 20 miles ; life-boats to save the crews of vessels in distress ; apartments for shipwrecked sailors ; and a constant patrol during stormy nights for 8 miles along the coast. Part of the funds are also employed to increase small benefices, to build and repair churches, to support schools, and to aid young men at the litdes. li. village, near the castle, was the i an old castle once the residence of the Northumbrian kings. Opposite B. Castle are the dangerous rocks called the Farn Isles, abounding in sea-fowL Here (irace Darling and her father saved the crew of the Forfarshire steamer in 1838.

bamian.c: BAMIA'N, a fruitful valley and pass of Afghanistan , about a mde in breadth, and enclosed by steep leading from Cabul to Turkistan. It is at an elevation of 84% feet, and is as yet the only known pass over the Hindu Kusli practicable for artillery ami heavy transport. This valley was one of the chief centres of Buddhist worship, as gigantic idols, mutilated indeed by fanatical Mussulmans, still remain to prove. B., with its colossal statues cut out in the rock, was described by the Buddhist monks who traversed Central Asia, on their way from China to India, in the 4th and 5th centimes. The statues are found on a hill about 300 feet high, in which are a multitude of cells excavated in the rock all round, and rising above one another in irregular tiers. The cells are covered with carving. The male figure is about 160 feet, the female, 120. Both are natural in attitude, and clothed in light drapery ; the face of the former is the most perfectly preserved. Each ligure is hewn out of a deep niche, also elaborately carved, and representing royal personages and a variety of symbols which resemble those on the cuius of the Sassanidae. Each contains a winding stair by which it is possible to ascend to the head. The whole valley is covered with the ruins of tombs, mosques, and other buildings, once belonging to the town of Ghulghuleh, which more recently occupied this site, and was destroyed by Genghis-Khan in 1221. Eight miles eastward of B. lies the ancient fortress of Zohak, attributed to the fabulous Persian Serpent-king of that name. The fortress is preserved for the purpose of guarding the important pass. Both there aud in the valley of B., a number of coins, ornaments, and other antiquities have been recently found, aud fully described by Masson, Wilson, Prinscp, Wood, and others. B.VMPTON, a small town in the north-east of Devonshire, chiefly on the left bank of the Batham, a tributary of the Exe, and 22 miles north of Exeter. There are lure extensive carboniferous limestone quarries. The manufacture of serge and pottery is carried on. St Michael's Church was built in the 1 1th >-.. and has a town- 70 ft. high. Pop. (1S71) 1111. !;\ MPTON IN Till-: RUSH, a smalltown in Oxfordshire, 14 miles south-west of Oxford. It has an ance iform church, with ■ Norman tower, and examples of every period of the point' d Qothic style. Pop. (1ST l ) 764

bamptonlectures.c:
BAMPTON LECTURES. These lectures are so called after the name of their founder, the Rev. John Bampton, Canon of Salisbury, who left estates originally worth £120 per annum, to the university of Oxford, for the endowment of eight divinity-lecture sermons, to be preached at '■ St Mary's every year, and to be published, at the expense of the estate, within two months of their being preached. The preacher is to lecture on one of the following subjects : The Confirmation of the Christian Faith, and the Confutation of all Heretics and Schismatics ; the Divine Authority of the Scriptures ; the Authority of the Primitive Fathers in Matters of Christian Faith and Practice; the Divinity of Christ ; the Divinity of the Holy < the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds. No person is qualified to preach these lectures who has not taken the degree of M.A., either at Oxford or Cambridge, and the same person shall never preach them twice. The first course was delivered in 17S0. In 1834 and 1835, no lecturers were appointed, and no lecture was preached in 1841. With these exceptions , there has been an unbroken series of very valuable, but rather learned than popular, discourses. The most remarkable are the following : Those delivered in 1784, on Christianity and Mohammedanism , by Dr White, who was accused of having obtained assistance in their composition from Dr Parr and Dr Badcock ; those by Dr Tatham in 1700, on the Logic of Theology; those of Dr Nott in 1802, on I ithiisiasm — this series noted against the pretensions of Wesley and Whitetield— those of Dr Maut in 1812 ; those of Id Heber in 1815; Whately in 1822; Milman in 1827 ; Burton in 1829, on the Heresies of the Apostolic Age; Soames in 1S30, on the Dor; of the Anglo-Saxon Church. But of the w series, none have caused greater excitement and controversy than those delivered by Dr Hampden in 1832, on 'The Scholastic Philosophy cons in its Relation to Christian Theology.' Hey were attacked on all sides, but especially by the leaders of the Oxford Tract Association. Hampdi a accused of Rationalism and Socmianism. When he was appointed Regius Professor of Divinity in 1836, a petition against his appointment was sent up to the throne; and upon this bein a censure was passed upon him in convocation by a largo majority, declaring his teaching to be unsound, and releasing undergraduates from attendance at his lectures. Notwithstanding this, lie was raised to the see of Hereford in 1S47, under tin- government of Lord John Russell — thirteen of the bench of bishops protesting against the appointment . There has been a recent course of B. I., delivered by Henry Longueville Mansel in 1858, on 'The Limits of Religious Thought,' which have caused a less bitter, but scarcely less interesting contr Mansel p p iww as a dialectician, and his lectures contained many very eloquent passages. The main p h he took up was, 'That the human mind inevitably, and by virtue of its essential constitution, tin. Is itself involved in self-contradictions whenever it ventures on certain cout rotation,' i. e, on Speculations C the infinite nature of God. He maintained that all attempts to oonstruot an objective or metaphysical the il >_y must neee- fail, and that tie- attainment of a philosophy of the Infinite is utterly impossible, under the ex. laws of human thought — tie- practical aim of the course being t-> shew the ' right use of reason in religious questions.' Mr Mansel was accused by ademning all dogma! (.-. »., all creeds and articles), and .-i mailing revelation itself impossible. Mr Maurice has been o his principal opponents. The B. L. ten red by < 1 ■■ R iwlinson, the > ig The - ( canon bullion's lectures in a our Lord's Divinity, have been the most important recently dalii A course of lectures similar to the Bampton was 65$

1 about the same time at Cambridge, bj the Rev. John llulse. See lit lskan la BAIT. Thu word occurs in most of the modern languages of Europe, and its primary signification appears to have been, 'to make a signal' (see Bahhbb), 'to proclaim' or 'publish.' This n ing it retains in the phrase, bans or banns (q. v.) of marriage. In Germany, the actu or / was a sentence of outlawry pronounced in the middle ost those who escaped from justice, or refused to submit to trial. We often read of i, and even cities, being placed under the ban i I Ire. The following are the terms of bannii a eo in an old formula: 'We declare thy wife a widow and thy children 01 we restore all thy feudal tenures to the lord of manor: thy private property we give to thy children; and we devote thy body and flesh to the ■ I-. ;t and the fowls of the air. In all ways and in every place where others find and safety, thou shalt find none; and we banish thee into the lour roads of the world — in the devil's name.' lit 1 sentences of outlawry, many other announcements were accompanied with denunciations and imprecations. When a grant of land was made fi lis purpo.se, or when a charter of lib ■ ranted, (In- transaction was proclaimed in public with certain ceremonies, and corses denounced against any one who should violate d. Thus banning, or publishing, came to be associated with cursing; and hence the origin of the popular use of the word. It occurs in this sense in Shakspeare and Milton, and other old writers.

bampura.c: BAMPU'RA, BHAMPUBA, or BHANPURA, a town of Hindustan, in the territoi-y of Indore, on the Rewa, 1.344 feet above the level of the sea, al)out ISO miles south-west of Gwalior. It is situated at the b.ise of a range of hills, is surrounded by a was, and has an unfinished fort, built of stone, which encloses an unfinished palace. Both palace and fort were begun by Jeswunt Row Holkar, of whom there is a beautiful marble statue in the palace. B. is the principal place of a pergninnah containing 70 villages. Pop. 20,009.

ban.c: BAN; ARRIERE BAIT. Besides the civil use of the word ban. as a proclamation or prohibition, there was a military application of the term in former days in France. When the feudal barons, who held their e tates and honours from the king, were summoned to attend him in the time of war. they were called the ban, or the levy first called out; the tenants, subordinate to these 1 f.ained the arri&re ban, or secondary levy.

BAN, or l'.A'XUS, supposed by some to be a contraction of the Dlyric word Bojan, i. ... lord, but more probably another form of the Slavonic word Pan, which possesses the same signification. Formerly, it was a title given to some of the military chiefs who guarded the eastern b iui dari of the Hungarian kingdom, and was therefore synonymous with the German Markgraf. The ban, who was appointed by the sovereign, but not for life, and whose appointment had to be ratified by the national diet, had originally very extensive, in fact, almost unlimited powers. In political, judicial, and military affairs, he was the supreme authority. With own territory, he exercised an influence similar to that of the l'alatiu in Hungary, and only lower than a king. In time of war, he headed the troops of his Banat (q. v.), and if the campaign occurred within its limits, it was his duty invariably to occupy the post of danger. lie led the van to battle, or covered the rear in retreat. For these services, he was recompensed partly in ready money, and partly by a monopoly of salt. The most important banats those of Dalniatia, Croatia, .Slavonia, Bosnia, Machow, and Szoreny, but their boundaries changed so frequently, that at the present day it is impossible to ascertain what they originally were. The encroachments of the Turks in the 16th c. rendered the union of the various banats necessary; an ' some time, the whole were formed into the double banat of Dalmatia and Croatia. A still more complete unity was subsequently obtained by centralising the military power. In 1723, the authority of the B. was made entirely subordinate to that of the 636 ivernment of Hungary. Afteo lu.les, his powers, rights, and titles were strictly denned during the reign of Maria Theresa, then acknowledged to Be the third dignitary of the Hungarian kingdom, appointed a membc t of the Hungarian council 0 stent, and pn of the council of the banat, and at the eor.inn the Hungarian king went before him, bearing the golden apple, the symbol ui\. Such was the position of the ban until the 4th of March 1S49, when Croatia, Slavonia, and Dalmatia were transformed into Austrian crown-lands, and the ban made wholly independent of Hungary, and endowed with the re powers as the governors of other crown-lands, but retaining, nevertheless, bis oj title. During the disturb in Vienna and Hungary, in 1848, the Ban Jellachich (q.v.) rei important service to the Austrian emperor.

banana.c: BANANA, a fruit originally East Indian, but much cultivated in warm countries over the whole globe. It is now generally regarded as a mere variety of the Plantain (q. v.); although they were formerly ranked by botanists as distinct species, the Plantain under the name of J/ / .. and the B. of M. sapientum — the specific name signifying 'of the wise men,' and being intended to convey an on to a statement by Theophrastus concerning a fruit which served as food for the wise men of India, and which, from his description, is sup] 1 to have been the plantain or banana. The names plantain and B. are somewhat vaguely used in their Banana. application to different cultivated varieties, which are very numerous ; those called B. have generally dark purple stripes and spots on their stems, and the fruit 1- smaller, less curved, and of more delicate taste than the plantain, with a soft and luscious pulp. Each fruit is generally about four or five inches long. The B. is always used in a ripe state, and never like the plantain, as a substitute for bread; unless when the pulp is squeezed thro fine sieve, and formed into small loaves, which, when dried, may be kept for a great length of time, but which are saccharine, and not farinaceous.
