BA'NKSIA, a genus of Australian shrubs of the natural order Proteacco: (q. v.), named in honour of Sir Joseph Ranks. A few of the species become small trees. They have hard dry leaves, generally white or very pale gn a beneath, and present a remarkable appearance from the umbellate arrangement of their branches, which bear towards their extremit: long heads of very numerous flowers. The flowers secrete much honey. Some of the species are now frequent ornaments of greenhouses in Britain. They are abundant in all parts Eanksia littoralis in tlower. Fruit and Leaf of Banksia, of Australia, forming, indeed, a characteristic feature of its vegetation, and are called Honeysuckle trees.

B. yrandia, found at Swan River, exceeds all the rest of the genua in size, attaining a height of 50 feet.

bann.c: BANN, the name of two riven to the north-east of Ireland ; the one, the Upper B., flowing into, and the other, the Lower B., out of Loch Neagh. The i B. rises on the north side of the Mourno Mountains, to the south of Downshire, and runs 25 miks north-north-west through the counties of Down and Armagh, successively in a granite, Silurian, trap, and tertiary basin, into the south side of Lough Neagh. It passes Banbridge, Gilford, and Portadown. At the latter place the Newry Canal joins it. The Lower B., strictly the continuation of the Upper, issues from the north-west corner of Lough Neagh, and flows 40 miles north-north-west, through Lough Beg, and dividing the counties of Antrim and Londonderry. It runs past Port- glenoue and Coleraine, into the Atlantic Ocean 4 miles south-west of Portrush. One mile above Coleraine it falls over a ledge of rock 13 feet high. It bears the surplus waters of Lough Neagh to the ocean, and has important salmon and eel-fisheries. Vessels of 200 tons can reach Coleraine by the river, 4 miles from the ocean.

bannatyneclub.c: BANNATYNE CLUB, a literary club deriving its name from George Bannatyne, to whose industry we are indebted for the preservation of much of the Scottish poetiy of the 15th and loth centuries. The J'.. C. was instituted in Edinburgh in 1823 by Sir Walter Scott, with the assistance chiefly of Mr David Laing of the Signet Library, Mr Archibald Constable , and Mr Thomas Thomson. The object of the institution was to print rare works illustrative of Scottish history, topography, poetry, miscellaneous literature, &c, in a uniform and handsome manner, either at the expense of the club, or as the contributions of individual members. As a general rule-, the number of copies of each work printed was limited to the number required for distribution among members, but in some instances a few were printed for sale. The club originally consisted of 31 members only, who paid an annual contribution of live guineas ; but owing to the anxiety of many eminent men to become members, the number was gradually extended to 100, where it was definitively fixed, the same annual payment being still required. Its I first president was Sir Walter Scott, and its first secretary Mr David Laing, who still continues to bhe duties of the office. The club had anmi:d meetings to December, which were of a very convivial character, so far as can be judged from an account of their first meeting published to the Edinburgh L tic of February 1824— afterwards reprinted by the club itself — which suggestively says that the Bannatyne Garland, No. 1, a song composed by one of the members, was sung 'to the tune of Four Boltles more.' meetings, however, have, within recent years, been given up; and the club itself, which, in 1859, cumbered about eighty memb . was to be dissolved in a few months. Since its commen it has numbered among its members many of the most distinguished Scotsmen, and has printed more than a hundred quarto works, besides several octavo ones, some valuable as they are rare, aud all bringing high prices at sales.

banner.c:
BA'NNER, a piece of cloth attached to a pole, and usually bearing BOme warlike or heraldic device, or national emblem. In this sense B. is a generic term, including many species, such as standard, ensign, pennon, flag, JtC. Banners have been used from the earliest times, and in all countries, for the purpose of directing the movements of troops. We read of them constantly to the Old Testament, as in Numbers ii. 2, ' Every man of the children of Israel shall camp by his standard, and under the i if his father's house.' The earliest Roman standard was a bundle of straw fixed to the top of a spear. This was succeeded by figures of animals — the horse, the boar, &c, all of which soon gave place t< i which continued all along to be the chief Roman ensign, and was afterwards assumed by the German, and latterly by the French emperors of the Napoleon dynasty. In addition to the eagle, each Roman cohort had a B., generally a serpent or woven on a square piece of cloth. The standard of the cavalry was a square piece of cloth expanded on a cross, and it was to this that the term vexillum properly applied. Examples of these standards are sculptured on the Arch of Constantine at Km., ..la from the Arch of Constantino. Rome. The top of the staff was also frcqi adorned with a figure of Mars or of Victory, and in later times, with the head of the reigning emperor. After Constantine embraced Christianity, the Cross was substituted for the head of the emperor on the purple B. of Byzantium. Standards were less in uso amongst the Greeks than has been usual with warlike nations ; but a standard, and sometimes a scarlet Hag, was employed as a signal for giving battle. On the rise of Chivalry, in the middle ages, the or. of banners, like every other branch of military organisation, attained "to something like scientific exactitude. From the B.-royal, which bore the national emblems, to the small .streamer attached to the lance, with its cross or stripes, there was a regular subordination, each emblem having its place and its meaning. The pennon of the simple knight 1 from the square P.. of the banneret (q. v.). ill I., in p itoti 1 at the ends. In addition to their varieties m i, and colour, these banners were distingui bed by the emblems which they bore. Ono'of the earliest is the Danish raven, depicted on th.' standard taken by Alfred, of which mentions the tradition, that ' to .very 1 wherever that flag want he. ' they [tho Danes] ■ o on tin- victory, a live crow would appear flying on the middle .if the flag ; but if they were doomed to I 1, it Would hang down motionless.' Nor did the privilege of carrying banners belong to princes and knights alone, bishops and abbots displayed similar ensigns, which were carried before them in religious j 671

and under which their retainers fought in their defence. It was to these that the term 'Gonfalon,' a word as to the origin of which much di\< commonly applied. In place of the emblems of the knight, the B. of the Chorda, and of t audi usually bore the effigies of Bairn . . '■■■ displayed do ensigns whatever, and were known simply by their colour. Of this the 01 or plain ruddy flag "f St Denis, was a famous example. The celebrated Bayeux Tapestry (q. v.) throws considerable light on banners, as well as on other matters conc (i,, | with the warlike arrangements of the middle Much curious information on this and kindred subjects will be found in Hewitfs I Armour and Weapons in Europe. By every warlike ] pie the B. has been regarded as the emblem of d honour, as a palladium for the defence of which the individual warrior was at all times ready to sacrifice his life. From the converse of this feeling, b and flags taken from the enemy have alwaj regarded as special trophies of victory, and places of honour in churches and public buildings have consequently been assigned them. As to the Eta borne by the ships of different nations, and the arrangements concerning them in peace and war, sec Flag; as to colours of regiment rs. The relation which banners bear to other kinds of flags, in their forms and uses will be explained undi c Colours, Regimental; Ensign; Flag: Pendant ; &c Banm r display/i d, is the term used by heralds to describe a 13. open and flying. BA'NXEBET, a higher grade of knighthood rred by the sovereign tor some heroic act performed in the field, and so called because the tin of the knight was then exchanged for the tanner — a proceeding which was effected by the very simple means of rending the points from the pennon. The first B. iu England is said by Froissart to have been made by King Edward I., and the last time the honour was conferred was by Charles I. after the battle of Edgeliill, the recipient being an individual who rejoiced iu the familiar nai John Smith. The ceremony of the creation of a Knight-B. must have been very impressive to pel ons tilled with the ideas which were prevalent in the ages of chivalry. The king, or his general, at the head of his army, drawn up in order of battle after a victory, under the royal standard displayed, attended by all the officers and nobility of the court, received the B. elect, who was not necessarily a knight previously, led between two its of note, or other men fane mis in arms, carrying his pennon in his hand, the heralds walking before him and proclaiming his valiant achievements , for which he deserved to be made a Knights ., and to display his banner in the field. The king, or general, then said to him : ' Advance, Banneret ! ' (AdvaTi Banneret), and caused the point of his pennon to be torn off. The new knight, with the trumpeters sounding before him, and the nobility and officers bearing him company, was sent back to his tent, where a noble entertainment was provided by the king. Seine attempts have been made to revive the title in recent tunes, as when George IU., at a review of the navy at Portsmouth in 177'!. conferred it on Admiral Pye and several other officers.

bannock.c: BA'NNOCK, a cake of home-mile bread, common in the country parts of Scotland, but now less so than formerly. It is usually composed oi meal or of pease and barley meal mixed; prepared without any leaven, it is baked on a circular plate of iron, called a girdle. When made of mixed meal, it is called a maahlum bannock ' Bannocks of meal' form ■ of a popular Scottish A superior bind of I'... culled a Selkirk B., Ero i the place where it is made, resembles the liner and 1 bter species of tea-cakes prepared by rd&is from the( west of Scotland, it is pronounced bunnock. 'Here is an amusing fairy-talc called 77 Story of the Wee (little) Bunnock. The B. is doubt!. it antiquity, being, in fact, the primitive cake, only varied in material, of every country.

bannockbltrn.c: BA'NNOCKBLTRN, a villa e in the ea Stirlingshire, I es* south-south-east of Stirling , on the Bannock rivulet, which falls, a few miles below this, into the Forth, Near this was fought the great battle of B. on Monday, 24th 1314. Robert Bruce, with 30,000 S i t< a, a signal victory over Edward II., with 100,000 English, and secured his throne and the independ- • ice of Scotland. The English are said to have 10,000, and the Scotch 8000 men. The 'Boro Stone,' on which Bruce is said to have fixed his standard on that eventful day, is still to be seen on an eminence near the sci ae of the fight. On the south-east of the field of B., at Sauchie Burn, James III. was defeateil in 14SS by his rebellious subjects, and assassinated after the battle iu a mill where lie had taken refuge. B. is now an important seat of the woollen manufactures, especially those of tartans and carpets. Jt has long supplied the tartan worn by the Highland regiments. Tanning is carried on to some extent, and the neighbouring 1 for the manufacture of Pop. 2627.

banns.c: BANNS, or BANS, in the law of England, means a proclamation, or public notification, or summons, in which general sac. however, it may be said to have become obsolete. It is now chiefly, if not solely, used in the publication of intended marriages, as to which, see next article.

BANNS or BANS OF MA'RRIAGE This] of three alternative preliminary forms now essential to the legal Celebration of marriage in England. The other two are marriage by licence, and marriage by a registrar's certificate. B. of M., like many of our ecclesiastics Ions, has its origin in the ancient practice of the Roman Catholic Church, which our reformers wisely refrained from abi ing. By the publication of these B. is meant the legal proclamation or notification within the parish, district, or chapelry, and in the proper church or chapel, of the names and descriptions of the pi wdio intend to be there married; tl bject I the notoriety of the solemn act, so that all who have objections to the marriage may be enabled to state them in time. According to the old English i law, the publication of B. might be made on but a change was made to Sundays by the £ t important Marriage Act, the 26 Geo. II. c. 3.'J; and although that act was afterwards superseded by the 4 Geo. IV. c. 76, the regulation as to Sundays has been since continued. The latter act is still the principal subsisting statute on the subject of marriage B., although it has lie 1 and extended by the 6 and 7 WilL IV. c. 85, the 1 Vic. c. 22, the 3 and -1 Vie. c. 72, fuel the 19 and 20 Vic-, c. 1 1 0. The law, as contained in these acts of parliament, is as follows : By the 4 Geo. IV. c. 7G, s. 2, it is enacted that all B. of matrimony shall be published in an audible manner, according to the prefixed to the marriage-sendee in the Bool: of Common Prayer, upon three Sundays preci the ceremony, during the time of morning-s. or of evening-service (if on the day of publication there shall be no morning-service) immediately after

the second lesson. The rubric referred to is in the following terms : ' I publish the banns of marriage between M. of and N. of . If any of you know cause or just impediment why these persons should not be joined together in holy matrimony, ye are to declare it. This is the first [second, or third] time of asking.' By the 22d section of the same act, all marriages celel without such publication of B., or without licence (or now, under the C and 7 Will. IV. c. 85, s. 42, without a Registrar's certificate), are declan d to be null and void. By the 26th section of the last- mentioned act, the bishop, with consent of the patron and incumbent, may license chapels for the celebration of marriages in populous places; and by the 33d section of the 1 Vic. c. 22, B. may be published in such chapels. By section 9 of the -1 Geo. IV. c. 76, it is provided, that if the marriage be not celebrated within three months after publication of B., the marriage shall not take mace until the B. shall have been republished on three several Sundays, unless it be a marriage by licence, or now, by certificate, which two latter alternatives, however, must also be availed of within the three months. It only remains to be added on the law, as contained in these marriage acts, that by section 8 of the last of them, the 19 and 20 Vic. c. 119, it is provided, that in every case in which one of the parties intending marriage without licence shall dwell in Scotland, a certificate of proclamation of B. in Scotland, under the hands of the session-clerk of the parish in which such proclamation shall have been made, shall, when produced to any person duly authorised under the provisions of this act to solemnise a marriage, be as valid and effectual for authorising such person to solemnise such marriage as the production of a certificate for marriage of a superintendent registrar of a district in England would be, in reference to a party it within such district. The purpose of the law is to secure public knowledge of intended marriages, and therefore, althouj : the 4 Geo. IV., following in this respect the 26 Geo. II., declares that marriages shall be void without publication of B. (where, of course, that is the chosen preliminary), it is not necessary that such publication should be made in the real baptismal names of both or either of the parties ; it is sufficient that the B. be published in the names by which the parties are known, or either of them. Nay, it even appears that where the baptismal names have been discovered, having been previously concealed OT unknown, it is better, if not necessary, that publication should be made in the names by which the parties are familiarly known in the district, by which, indeed, they may be said to be known to the world. There are numerous cases decided in England from which such doctrine necessarily follows . In one of these cases, Lord Chief-justice Ellenborough, the highest judicial authority that could be named, stated, in giving judgment: 'The object of the act is to secure notoriety, to apprise all persons of the intention of the parties to contract marriage ; and how can that be better attained than by publication in the names by which parties are known ? I think that the act only meant publication by known and acknowledged names.' It has also he, D decided, that a fraudulent knowledge of a wrong name in the publication of B. will not void the marriage, unless the fraud should be on both side.-!. In Scotland. B. have the same Roman Catholic origin as in England. Indeed. Mr Erskine, one of tip most authoritative Scotch legal writers, gives it as Ins opinion, that the Scotch borrowed the practice from the decrees of the Council of Trent; but a recent able writer (see Frasers Domestic Relations, vol. i. p. 113) considers this opinion erroneous, and shews that B. were first sanctioned in Scotland by councils which were held in that country long of the Council of Trent. After the Reformation in Scotland, tin practice of proclaimine B., as the phrase is in that country, was continued. They are described in the Scotch Act 1661, c. 34, ' ;us a part of the laudable order and constitution of the kirk ;' and they have since been mentioned in various acts of parliament applicable to Scotland, 9 the 10 Anne, c. 7, and the 4 and 5 Will. IV. c. 28. By the first of these acts, the privi! publicly celebrating marriage was extended to the Scotch Kpisi-upnltaii clergy, but with a proviso that the B. should be duly published three Lord's Days, not only in the Episcopal churches which the parties frequent, but also in the parish church or churches. Should the parish minister, however, neglect or refuse to publish the B. of such parties, the act declares that it shall be sufficient to do so in any Episcopal congregation alone. The 4 Will. IV. c. 28, puts other dissenting bodies in Scotland in the Bame position as the Episcopal Church there ; but there is this little difference, that publication of the B. of such dissenters is required to be made in the parish church alone. There is one other regulation of the Scotch law on this subject which is deserving of notice for popular information — namely, that when both of the parties have their domicile (q. v.) within Scotland, and enter into marriage in England or Ireland, they must have their B. proclaimed in the parish church of their domicile in Scotland, otherwise they are liable to the penalties of clandestine marriage. Such is the express enactment of the Scotch statute 1661, c. 34. The Scotch law differs from the English in regard to the effect of non-publication of bums. In England, as we have seen, the consequence is to render the marriage absolutely void. In Scotland, however, marriage, without proclamation of B., is valid ; but in such case the parties, celebrator, and witnesses are liable in the above penalties. See Marriage Licence, Si>ecial Licence, Ro Certificate.

banquette.c: BANQUETTE, in Fortification, is a raised ledge or step inside the parapet of a rampart, of such a height that musketeers, when standing on it, may be able to fire over the crest of the parapet without too much exposure to the enemy. It is about 4 feet wide, and 4 or 4f feet below the crest. The musketeers ascend to it from the rampart either by a few steps or by a sloping path.

banswakra.c:

asociulency of the Maliraltas, by ^^ lioni it was fearfully o[>pres.see.l. In 1S12, the ruler made overtures to the British government, offering to become tributary on condition of iirotection ; anil an arransenieut to this effect was concluded in 181S. — The ea|pital, also called Banswarra, is on the route from ftlhow to Decsa, 12.'i miles north-west from Mliow. The majority of the inhabitants are Hindus, but the Mussulmans are also pretty numerous. The ii.alace of the ]!awul, or chief, is a large, turreted, battle- mcnted building, on a rising ground overlooking the town, near a beautiful tank, overhung with trees.

bantam.c: BANTA'M, a seaport, now decayed, in a district of the same name, which forms the west end of .lava. It is 4(1 miles to the west of Batavia. being in lat. 6° 2' S.. and long. 106° 11' E. It was foe by the Dutch in 1602, being their i iblish- ment in the island. The district contains 362.242 inhabitants.

bantamfowl.c: BA'NTAM FOWL, a well known variety of the common Domestic Fowl (q. v.), originally brought from the East Indies, and supposed to derive its name from Bantam, in Java. It is remarkable for small size, being only about a pound in weight, and for a disposition more courageous and pugnacious than even that of a game-cock. A bantam-cock will drive to a respectful distance great dunghill-cocks five times its weight, and has been describ ' a beautiful example of a great soul in a little body.' Tlere arc several subvarieties of the bantam. Most of them ha\ much feathered. The flesh and eggs are g lod, although the eggs are of course small ; and the bantam lavs well in winter. 673

Bondman), a • of 0« (q. v.), a native of Java an. 1 I which, in. colour, shape, horns, ami want of d bears some resemblance to tin' Qm (q. v.) of India, ' hut in the skeleton of the gaur, the sacrum conof 5 vertebra, and the tail of 10, while in tin' skeleton of the 1'.., the sacrum consists of bu( 4 vertebra?, and the tail of 18.' The B. is black, with white hair is short ami sleek, i limbs slender. The muzzle is sharp. The rises into a high arch immediately behind the > The B. inhabits forests, ami has been generally described as untamable, but this opinion rests on no satisfactory authority. BA'STKY, a seaport town in the south-west of Cork county, Ireland, in a cove opposite Whidd at the head of B. Bay, and 44 miles west-south-wi it of Cork. The two chief streets converge i open space towards the sea, and mountains, '.Ki.'! fet rise behind the town. The chief trade is the export of agricidtural produce. A little ashing is carried on. In last century, there was an extensive pilchard-fishery here ; but the pilchard has now deserted the coast. Many tourists resort to B. in summer. Pop. between 2IHHI ami 3000.

bantrybay.c: BA'NTRY BAY, a deep inlet in the south-west extremity of Ireland, between Crow Point and Sheep's Head Point, in Cork county. It is 25 miles long, running east-north-east, with a breadth of 3 to 5 miles. It is one of the finest harbours in Europe, affording safe and commoiUous anchorage for ships of all sizes. Near the entrance on the north side is a line large sheltered harbour, formed by Bear Island, with a safe passage on both sides. At the head of the bay are two harbours : the one to the south, or the landlocked roadstead of B. harbour, is formed by Whiddy Isle, opposite B. town; the other to the north, or Glengariff harbour, is also sheltered by an island, but is small, and narrow at the entrance. The coast around B. B. is rocky and high, consisting of Devonian strata, and exhibiting some of the finest scenery in the kingdom. On the north side, 17 miles west of B. town, is tie cataract of Hungry Hill, where three lakes, at the heights of 1011, 1126, and 13G0 feet above the sea, discharge their waters, by almost continuous c:e into Adrigoole Creek Near the opening of B. B. a skirmish took place, in 168ft between a small b fleet under Admiral Herbert (afterwards Lord Torrington), and the French fleet, which conveyed James IL to Kinsale. Several ships of the French invading expedition under General Hoche anchored here in 1796.

banxring.c: BANX'RING (Tupaia), a genus of insectivorous quadrupeds, remarkably differing from the other insectivora (q. v.) in their habits, as they din trees with the agility of lemurs or squirrels. They are also remarkable for their very elongated muzzle. They have soft glistening fur, and a long bushy tail. The few species known are all natives of the Indian archipelago.

banyan.c: BA'NYA (Xf.may), or NEU'STADT, a town of Hungary, province Szathmar, with a royal mint, and productive mines of gold and silver. Pop. 5500.

BANYAN, or BATTCAN (Ficus Indica), a tree, native of India, remarkable for its vast rooting branches. It is a species of Fie (q. v.) ; has ovate, heart-shaped, entire leaves, about live or six inches long ; and produces a fruit of a rich scarlet colour, not larger than a cherry, growing in pairs from the axils of the leaves. The branches send shoots downwards , which, when they have rooted, become stems, the tree in this manner spreading over a great surface , and enduring for many ages. One nas been described as having no fewer than 350 stems, equal to Urge oaks, and more than 3000 s; covering a space sufficient to contain 7000 persons. The branches are visually covered with monkeys, ind enormous bat . The m the fruit and leaves. The vegetation of the B. i ins on the ground. The seeds are ed by birds in the crowns of palms, and send down roots which embrace and eventually kill tho palm. As the B. gets old, it breaks up into separate masses, the original trunk decaying, and the props becoming separate trunks of the different portions. The wood of the B. is light, porous, and of no value. The bark is regarded by the Hindoo physicians as a powerful tonic, and is administered in diabetes. The white glutinous juice is used to relieve toothache , and also as ion to the soles of the Eeet when inflamed. Bird-lime is also made from it. Gum-lac is obtained in abundance from the B.-tree. The B.-tree is beautifully described by Southey in his poem The Curse of Keltama.

banyulssurmer.c: BANYULS-SUR-MER, a town of France in the Pyrenees Orientates, with a fishing-port on the Mediterranean. The celebrated wines of Grenache and liancio are produced in this district. Near the town are four old towers, one of which marks tho division between France and Spain. B. was the immediate scene of many encounters between tho French republicans and the Spaniards during the first French Revolution. Pop. (1872) -2227.

banyuwangy.c: BANYUWA'NGY, or BANJO UVA-NGY, an important and populous seaport town and military post belonging to the Dutch, on the cast coast of Java, capital of district of same name.

bapaume.c: BAPAUME, a fortified town of France, department of Pas-de-Calais. A portion of the allied troops advanced to this place after compelling the French to abandon their fortified position, and to retreat behind the Scarpe, in August 1793. Pop. 2S64.

baphomet.c:
BA'PHOMET is the name of a mysterious symbol, which was in use among the Templars. According to the oldest and most probable interpretation , the word is a corruption of Mahomet, to whose faith the members of the order were accused of having a leaning. The symbol consisted of a small human figure cut out of stone, having two heads, male and female, with the rest of the body purely feminine. It wa3 environed with serpents, and astronomical attributes, and furnished with inscriptions for tho most part in Arabic. S[>ecimens are to be found in the archaeological collections of Vienna and Weimar. Hammer, however, in his Fundgruben des Orients, derives B. from Gr. baphi, baptism; and metis, council or

wisdom. He charges the knigbta with a depraved Gnosticism, and makes the word signify the baptism of wisdom — the baptism of fire; in short, the Gnostic baptism — a species of spiritual illumination, which, however, was interpreted sensually by later I cs, such as the Ophites (an Egyptian sect of the 11th a), to whose licentious practices he declares them to have, been addicted. But this explanation is generally discredited.

baptism.c:
BA'PTISM (Gr. baplo, to dip or wash, or to stain with a liquid), one of the sacraments (q. v.) of the ' tn Church, deriving its name from the outward rite of washing with water, which forms ential part of it. B. is almost universally 1 d il among Christians as a sacrament, and is referred to the authority of Christ himself, whose express commandment is recorded in the Is (Mat. xxviii. 19; Mark xvi. 16). B. is frequently mentioned in the New Testament as a divine ordinance. The name and the rite were not, however, i her new when the ordinance was instituted by Christ. Religious meanings were early attached to washings with water, both by heathens and Jews ; they were among the ordinances of the Jewish law ; and it is not necessary to go beyond that law to find the origin of the custom of washing or baptising proselytes upon their admission into the Jewish Church. Washing with water was requisite for the removal of ceremonial uncleanness , and every proselyte must have been ted as, prior to his admission into the Jewish i, ceremonially unclean. John the 1; baptised not proselytes upon their renouncing heathenism and entering the Jewish Church, but those who, by birth and descent, were members of it, to indicate the necessity of a purification of the soul from sin — a spiritual, and not a mere outward change. One of the most important of the controversies which have agitated the Christian Church as to Bl, is that concerning the proper subjects of B., whether adults only who profess faith in Christ are to be baptised, or if this ordinance is to be administered to their infants also. See Baptists, and Baptism, Infant. The B. of adults was certainly more frequent in the apostolic age than it has ordinarily been where the B. of infants has prev .iii 1 ; for which an obvious cause presents itself in the fact, that the first members of churches were converts from Judaism or from heathenism. It is, however, generally held by those who advocate the B. of infants, that it was the practice of the apostles and of the church of the apostolic age to baptise the infants of Christians; which, on the other hand, is as stoutly denied, and infant B. is alleged to have crept in along with other corruptions . For neither opinion can any positive historical proof be adduced, the arguments on both sides being purely inferential. It is admitted, on all hands, that at an early period in the history of the church, B. was administered to infants, although, according to ler, even after 'it had been set forth as an apostolic institution, its introduction into the general practice of the church was but slow.' He finds ' the first trace ' of it in Irenseus. It was opposed by Tertullian about the end of the '2d c. ; and was advocated by Cyprian, and acknowledged as an apostolic institution in the North African Church and in the Alexandrian and Syro- Persian Churches in the 3d c. ; but it was not until the 5th c. that it became fully established as the general practice of the Christian Church. It has unquestionably continued to be the general practice from that period to the present day ; feebly opposed by some of the sects of the middle ages, and more rigorously by some of those who have adopted the general principles of the Reformation. h the practice of infant B., and the neglect of it in the early ages of the church, were connected with particular views of religious doctrine, and of the nature and purpose of B. itself. The prevalence of the Augustinmn doctrine of original sin is generally regarded as a principal cause of the nee of infant B. ; but Pelagius, whilst opposing that doctrine, maintained the necessity of infant B., apparently upon the ground that the kingdom of heaven can be attained by human beings only through God's •rice. No little influence in favour of infant B. must be ascribed to the growing belief of the absolute necessity of B. to salvation, and of a sort of mysterious efficacy in the rite itself. It is certain, on the other hand, that the in the forgiveness of sins in B. led to a practice of deferring it as long as possible, that all sins might be blotted out at once ; thus the Emperor Constantine the Great was baptised only a short time before hi3 death. The approach of a war or pestilence caused many to rush forward in ba.,tc to be baptised, who had previously delayed. Two modes of B. are practised by immersion or dipping, and by aspersion or sprinkling, concerning winch there has been much controversy in the early period of the church's history, as well as in recent times. Affusion, or pouring, the common practice of the Church of Rome, may be regarded as essentially the same with sprinkling. The advocates of sprinkling universally admit the validity of B. administered in the other mode, but the advocates of dipping generally refuse to acknowledge that B. by sprinkling can be true Christian baptism. The opponents of infant B., almost without exception, insist upon immersion ; whilst aspersion or affusion of water is general, except in the Eastern ebm wherever the B. of infants prevails. The argument upon which Baptists depend most of all is from the word B., and the verb baplho, to baptise, which also, in classic Greek, signifies to immerse. On the other side, it is contended that a strict limitation to this sense does not well accord with its character as a 'frequentative' form of baplo . instances are I from the New Testament itself, in which this signification cannot easily be attached either to the noun or to the vci 1 Cor. x. 2, where Paid says that the Isr were 'baptised unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea;' ami Heb. ix. 10. Mark vii. 4, and xi. 38, where both verb and noim are employed concerning the tcashings of the Jews, and the noun even of their washing of 'cups, and pots, brazen . and of tables.' — To the argument in favour of immersion, derived from the phrases eni] il when B. is mentioned in Scripture, as when we are told (Mat. iii. G) that John the Baptist baptised 'in Jordan,' that our Lord after his B. (Mat. iii. 10) ' went up out of the water,' that Philip and the Ethiopian eunuch (Acts viii. .'IS) 'went down both into the water ; ' it is replied that all the passages of this description, even if their meaning were certainly as precise and full as Baptists suppose it to be, are insufficient to sustain the weight of the conclusion as to the necessity of a particular mode of B. ; that, however, it is far from being clear that these passages must be interpret. ,1 or the meaning of the prepositions so strictly defined as the argument requires; and further, that there are in>; mentioned in Scripture which afford a presumptive argument in favour of another mode of i where we ar rest numbers added to the church in one day; whilst we have nowhere any

intimation of converts being led to any pond or river to I* baptised. To the argument drawn from the language of Paul in Bom. vi. 4, Col. ii. 12 (see Baptists), it is replied that it depends upon a fanciful interpretation of these texts. — Ace to most of tl»- advocates of P>. by sprinkling, the great error of their opponents is that of at I too much importance to the question of the mode of baptism. It is, however, indisputable that in the primitive church the ordinary mode of li. was by immersion, in order to which Baptisteries (q.v.) began to be erected in tho .'id, perhaps in the 2d c, and the sexes were usually baptised apart. But B. was administered to sick persons by sprinkling; although doubts as to the complete efficacy of tins (sick) B. were evidently prevalent in the time of Cyprian (middle' of 3d c). 1!. by sprinkling gradually Became more prevalent; but the dispute e hi in i | the mode of P.. became one of the irreconcilable differences between the Eastern ail Western Churches, the former generally adhering to the practice of immersion, whilst the latter adopted mere pouring of water on the head, or sprinkling on the face, which practice has generally ]n< since the 13th c. ; but not universally, for it was the ordinary practice in England before the lU'forma- tion to immerse infants, and the funis (q. v.) in the churches were made large enough for this purpose. This continued also to be the practice till the reign of Elizabeth ; and the change which then took place is ascribed to the English divines who had sought refuge in Geneva, and other places of the continent, during the reign of Mary. To this day the rubric of the I 'hurch of England requires, that if the godfathers and godmothers ' shall certify him that the child may well endure it,' the officiating priest 'shall dip it in the water discreetly and warily ; ' and it is only 'if they shall certify that the child is weak,' that 'it shall suffice to pour water upon it,' which, however, or sprinkling, is now the ordinary practice. B. was accompanied, from an early period in the history of the church, with various forms and ceremonies , besides the simple rite of washing with water and the pronouncing of the fornuda which declares it to be 'in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.' These ceremonies are almost all retained in the Church of Borne, and also generally in the oriental churches, but have been entirely or almost entirely laid aside by Protestants. The Church of England retains the sign of the cross made upon the forehead alter B., but the other Protestant churches in Britain reject it. It was an ancient custom that the riilir/iunu-iis, as candidates for B. were called whilst receiving instruction with a view to that sacrament, when they were to be baptised, publicly made a profession of their faith and a renunciation of the devil and all his works. The profession of faith is still retained by Protestant churches as the formal ground of the administration of B. ; the renunciation of the devil and bis works is required by the Church of England of the person baptised, if an adult, or of the sponsors or ' sureties ' of a child.— Sponsors (q. v.) were early admitted to answer for those who could not answer for themselves , and particularly for infants. The belief in the absolute necessity of B. to salvation led even to B. of the dead among the Montanists (q.v.) in Africa, in which sponsorship was also introduced. Presbyterian and Independent churches generally reject all sponsorship, and regard the profession made by parents as simply a profession of their own faith, which entitles their infants to baptism. The ancient practice of exorcism (q. v.) immediately before B. has been rejected as superstitious by almost all Protestant churches ; as have also 676 that of immersing three times (trine immersion), or sprinkling three times, with reference to the three persons of the Godhead — that of brei upon the baptised person, 'to signify th • I ipuls OH of the devil,' and to symbolise the gift of the Holy .Spirit — that of anointing with oil ., v.), to symbolise the same gift, or to indicate that the baptised person is ready, as a wrestler in the ancient , to light the good light of faith — that of giving him milk and honey, in token of his spiritual youth, and of his reception of spiritual gifts and graces — that of putting a little salt into bis mouth, to signify the wisdom and taste for heavenly this prop r to a Christian— that of touching his nostrils and ears with spittle, to signify that his ear; are to be ever open to truth, and that he should ever feel the sweet odour of truth and virtue— and that of clothing him after B. with a white robe (the chry- tome), in token of the innocence of sold which by B. he was supposed to have acquired. The white robe and the anointing with oil were retained in the Church of England for a short time after the Reformation. — The giving of a name in B. (see Names, Baptismal) is no essential part of it, but is a custom apparently derived from that of the Jews in circumcision (Luke i. 59— G3). — The Church of Rome prefers the use of holy- water (q.v.) in B., but regards any water as fit for the purpose in i necessity. — According to an ancient usage, long obsolete , the ordinary administration of B. was limited to the two great festivals of Easter and Whitsuntide. — Whether B. may In red in private, has been much debated, both in ancient and modern times. The administration of B. in private houses, and not in the presence of a congregation, was one of the i I earnestly contended against by the Presbyterians in Scotland in the first half of the 17th c. ; their opposition being grounded, not only upon hostility to what they deemed usurpation of authority, but upon the danger of superstitious views of baptism. And apparently upon this latter ground, B. in private houses is also discouraged, even while it is allowed, if there is ' great cause and necessity,' by the Church of England; yet it has become very frequent both in 1 1 1. I hurch of England and among the Presbyterians of Scotland. Some of the most important questions concerning B. will be most appropriately noticed in the article ment, particularly those relating to its place in the Christian system and among the means of grace. The opinions early became prevalent, that forgiveness of sins is obtained in B., and spiritual life begun, and that it is indispensably necessary to salvation — exception being only made, if any was made at all, of the case of believers, adult persons, who desiring B.,Were prevented from being baptised, and particularly of those who suffered martyrdom, which was generally held to be equivalent to baptism . The Church of Rome still owns, as supplying the place of B. by water, these two — B. by d and J!, by blood — i. e., in martyrdom. According to the general doctrine of the Protestant churches, B. is 'a sign and seal' of the covenant of gj ■■■, representing as a sign the blessings of the covenant, and as a seal, confirming the covenant. As a sign, it is generally held to represent in its rite of washing, the removal both of guilt and corruption, by the ljlood and by the Spirit of Clirist, and so to relate equally to pardon and regeneration, although some have limited its symbolic reference to regeneration alone. One of the most important points disputed concerning B., is that of baptismal regeneration . See Regeneration. Some early Christian sects appear to have rejected B., ou grounds somewhat simUar to those on which it is rejected by Quakers (q.v.) at the present day,

who explain the passages which relate to it symbolic ritual I'., is tli" only real B. of Christians, The Socinians (oyv.) si modern times have maintained that B. is not an ordinance of permanent obligation, but a merely symbolical rite of little importance. Much controversy has taken place concerning Ley ..;. Wherever there is a recognised ministry in the church, there is a general agreement in referrin" the ordinary administration of B. to those who hold office. It might be expected that the more strongly the necessity of the transmission of holy orders by apostolical succession is asserted, the more strongly also would ezclnsiveness be manifested with regard to the right of the der<)y to administer B. liut this tendency is counteracted by the belief in the necessity of B., or at least of its great importance to I he tlvation of infants; so that from an early period lay B. was allowed, although not without a struggle, in im .11 :ipprehenileil danger; and in the Church of Borne, this principle is logically carried out to the fullest extent, and even women are authorised to administer B. in cases of necessity, tin the same ground, lay B. was at first permitted in the Protestant Church of England ; but the prevalence of other views led to a kind of formal restriction of the right of administering it to 'lawful mini although in practice the validity of lay B. is still generally recognised. Another question much agitated in the church from early times, is that concerning the validity of B. by heretics. The opinion ultimately prevailed, that B. by heretics is valid, except in the case of those who do not baptise in the name of the three Persons of the Godhead. This continues to be the almost universal opinion. Few Protestant theologians hesitate to acknowledge the validity of B. administered in the Church of Rome. The B. of Mis is a custom supposed to have been introduced about the 10th ft, and still retained in the Church of Rome. The term benediction is sometime! substituted for I!.; but the rite itself is very similar to that of B., and is accompanied with many similar ceremonies — 'a sort of exorcism,' sprinkling with holy-water, anointing ' with the oil of catechumens ' and ' with chrism,' a formula of consecration 'in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost,' and sometimes also, if not always, the giving of a name to the bell consecrated, and even a kind of sponsorsliip as by godfathers and godmothers in baptism. This custom has no doubt greatly fostered the notion of an efficacy in the ringing of bells for protection in storms, and Car other benefits; indeed.it is expressly avowed that ' the bells arc blessed, to turn off storms and tempests from the faithful.'

BAPTISM, INFANT. The chief arguments in favour of infant B. are based upon the proposition that the church is one throughout all changes of dispensation. From this it is argued that as infants were, so they still must be included in the visible church. It is maintained that in all covenants which God has made with men, their children have been included; that the covenant with Abraham was a renewed revelation of the covenant of grace, lli temporal promises made to him being connected with the greatest spiritual promises; that circumcision was a seal of the covenant with respect to these, in which the children of Christians have the same interest that Jewish children had; and that B. is a seal of the covenant now as circumcision was. the things to which it has immediate reference i also blessings which children are capable of. It is contended that the arguments in favour of infant salvation derive additional strength from that view of the place of infants in the church according to which they are entitled to baptism. ; issages which connect B. with faith are I ively relating to adults, like the passages which connect salvation with faith and repentance. In reply to the argument that there is no express command for infant B., it is argued that the state of the case rather demands of who oppose it the production of an express command against it, without which the general command must be held to include it ; the words and actions of our Saviour (Mark x. 14) with respect to children are quoted as confirming the opinion that the place of infants in the church is precisely what it was under the Jewish dispensation; and it is contended that it would have been a very great restriction of pi i , in the new dispensation if infants had been ex. from a place which they held before, as entitled to a seal of the covenant, whereas it is evident that the new dispensation is characterised not by restriction I nit by enlargement of privilege. — Those who hold the doctrine of infant B. are styled Pa-do- baptists. The Roman Catholic and Lutheran Churches regard the B. of infants as admitting them mi i the church, and making them members of Christ's body. The Reformed (q. v.) Churches hold that the children of Christians are included in the visible church from their birth, and therefore entitled to baptism. These are the natural starting-points of very different systems.

baptistery.c:
BA'PTISTERY (Gr. baptisterion, a large vase or basin), the name given sometimes to a separate building, sometimes to the portion of the church itself in which the ceremony of baptism was performed . In the latter case, the B. was merely the enclosure containing the font, to be seen in most English churches. According to the earlier arrangements of the Christian Church, however, the B. seems usually to have been a building standing Section and Plan of Baptistery at A ti. detached from, though in the immediate vicinity of the church to which it appertained. Baptisteries, at first, were either hexagonal or octagonal, but afterwards became polygonal, and even circular. The B. of St Giovanni in Fonte, at Rome, commonly know n as the B. of ( 'onstantine, is octagonal, whilst the church of St Constantia, which was originally a B., is circular. The celebrated B. of Florence is an octagonal structure, measuring about one hundred feet in diameter. It stands detached from, but in the immediate vicinity of the cathedral. It is built of black and white marble, in the style which Giotto is said to have introduced, and which is still peculiar to Florence. Internally, a gallery, which runs nearly round the whole building, is supported by sixteen large granite columns, and the vaulted roof is decorated with mosaics by Andrea Tali, the pupil of Cimabue. Rut the magnificent Irene dei.is. with their beautiful bas-reliefs, are the most remarkable feature of this famous baptistery. The most celebrated of the three doers was executed by Lorenzo Ghiberti, the earliest being 6? 7

' . i idrea of 1'isa. Fifty years were required for their completion; audit is remarkable that the i fca for their execution are still preL Next in importance, and of even I the B. of l'isa. It is circular in form, the ter measuring 11G feet. Externally, it is 1 into three stories, the two under ones being surrounded by columns, of which the upper are smaller and more numerous than the under. The buildim; is raised from the ground on three and terminates in a pear-shaped dome, which is famous for its echo, the side. whispering- galleries. The largest B. ever el to hive been that of St Sophia, at Constantinople, which IS as to h:i\ on one occasion for the residence of the Emperor Basibcus.

baptists.c:
BAPTISTS (sometimes called AiUipcedol as opposed to Pa who advocate Infant Baptism*). This denomination of Christians refuse to acknowledge any great name OS founder of their sect. They trace their origin to the primitive church itself, and refer to the Acts of the Apostles and their Epistles as affording in their opinion, incontestable evidence that their leading tenet- had the sanction of inspiration. When Christianity became corrupted by the rise o£ Antichrist, they point to the maintenance of their scripture practice : tbe C'athari and Alhigenscs and other sects of the middle ages, who, in the midst of surrounding darkness, continued to hold fast the apostolic testimony. They sprung into notice in England under Henry VIII. and Elizabeth. They were persecuted under both reigns, but tbey received freedom to meet for worship from James II.. and com] ill is liberty under William III. Ever since, they have diffused their principles extensively in ( treat Britain and North America ; many of their XS have done good service to the cause of science and literature, and, both as preachers and writers, have taken a position of eminence in society. The B. hold the plenary inspiration and supreme authority of the Holy Scriptures as a revelation from < rod ; the equal deity of the Son and the Holy Spirit in the unity of the ever blessed Trinity. But, as a condensed view of opinions cannot be e >. | in this work, it may be as well to state that the denomination are distinguished by almost all the Bhades of belief which exist in other bodies. They have among them Calvinists both hyper and moderate, also high and low Arminians, di\ off in every variety of shade from a common centre. The great body of them in Britain and America hold the doctrine of Calvinism in a modified form; that is to say, they maintain the sufficiency of the Atonement for all men, the limitation for which some have pleaded, they consider, lies in its a tion to the sinner by the sovereign grace of God through faith. They maintain the nece regeneration and holiness of life as essential to true religion, and that 'without holiness no man shall see the Lord ; ' and their conduct, in general, will bear a ci mparison with any class of their co-religionists. /• B., so called because holding that Christ died for an elect number, and i B., who maintain that he died for all men, constitute the two hading sects into which the body is divided. English B., in their church order and government, are the same as Congregationahsts, the * The Baptists of Great Britain and America reject the name of Anabaptists, as expressing only an accidental oircni of their tenets— viz., the rebaptisinp; of converts from other sects, who happen to have been baptised in infancy, and also as iting them with the scandals of the German An i "f the loth c., from whom they claim to be hist From the same feeltnff, the modern sect in Germany and Upland style themselves Taufgesiunte. 67S J baptism excepted. Scotch B., properly so I on a plurality of pastors in every church, and the exercise of mutual exhortation by the members in their public assemblies. There ate Baptist churches in England, however, who are Scotcli in their order, and English B. in Scotland who are English in theirs. Seventh-day B., we believe, are to be found almost wholly in America, who observe not the first day of the week, but the seventh, as a day of rest. There are, besides these peat divisions, various small associations of B. scattered over Great Britain, America, and the continent of Europe, whose opinions cannot be gathered up into systematic arrangement, and who woidd not approve of being identified with any of I arian designations here set down. The particular tenet which characterises B. among their fellow-Christians is, that baptism is an ordinance the validity of which depends on an intel- bgeut faith on the part of the recipient. Their views on the matter of baptism may !• two beads — the subjects and mode of baptism. The subjects of the baptismal rite they hold to be bebevers in the Lord Jesus Christ. They ground their faith in this matter on the following tions — namely: 1st, The Lord in his commission to his apostles associates teaching with baptism, and limits the administration of the rite to Me taught 2d, The Acts of the Apostles shews how I they understood their Master, for they b none but bebevers, or such as appeared to be so. 3d, That the kingdom of Christ as it appears in this world is restricted to credibly converted persons , as is shewn in bis discourse with Nicodemus : ' Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God;' and his subsequent statements on to the hour when be emitted his memorable confession before Pilate, 'My kingdom is not of this World,' uniformly proves that its subjects an i tutes form a distinct and separate community from the Jewish theocracy, which embraced parents and en in nonage in one common weal th. 4th, They maintain that the ordinance, as explained in the New Testament, always point i to a moral and spiritual change, apart from which it were indeed a meaningless ceremony. As respects the mode, the B. hold that only immersion in water is baptism. They argue, that the original term baptizo conveys this meaning, and no other; that nothing less can possibly answer to the apostle's explanation in Korn. vi. 4, 5, and CoL ii. 12, ' buried with him in baptism, wherein also yo are risen with him;' that the many allusions in the epistles to the churches manifestly bear out this interpretation ; and, finally, that the fact of John baptising at a spot selected for the purpose ' because there was muclt water there,' is perfectly conclusive. Their form of church-government is congregational. They maintain that the only order of officers remaining to tbe church, since inspiration ceased, are pastors (otherwise called elders and bishops), deacons, and evangelists ; that the number of official persons in each of the apostolic churches cannot be ascertained from the record, but must of necessity have depended — and always must depend — on circumstances ; that each church is possessed of the power of self-government under its exalted head, Jesus Christ, subject to no foreign tribunal or court of review ; that discipline is to be exercised by the rulers in presence, and with the consent of all the members, and parties received or excluded at then- voice. The B. are divided among themselves regarding communion — one portion receiving conscientious 1'a.dobaptists to the Lord's table and membership ;

the other refusing this privilege to any but Baptists. The churches of the former are called open com- munionists; the latter, strict coram Next to the Moravians, the B. were earliest in the field of missions. They have been honour d ' I plant Christian churches in many parts of continental India, in Ceylon, in the Bahamas, th Indies, Africa, and China. No mission hand has arisen in any denomination, within the century, who have the agents of the Baptist Missionary Society in ardent zeal, patient perseverance, and invincible fortitude, in carrying out their Lord's commission to preach the gospel to every creature. The names of Carey, Marshman, Ward, and Knibb will be had in grateful remembrance by all succeeding generations ; and their footsteps are now being trod by a long list of Christian missionaries of all evangelical persuasions, who are ' the messengers of the churches and the glory of Christ.' This section of the Christian church was probably less zealous than their brethren, at one time, in preparing their ministers for their work by a sound course of study in theology and general literature; but this reproach has been long rolled away. They have schools of learning inferior to none for training young men of piety for pastoral duties, presided over by men of great ability. At Bristol, Bradford, Regent's Park (London), Pontypool, Haverf <■: and Nottingham, there exist seminaries of learning which are entitled to give certificates qualifying for matriculation at the university of London ; and many of the students have already taken degrees and honours there. In 1870, the B. of the United States had 17,745 churches, and 1,410,493 members. In 1872, the B. gland had 4013 churches and chapels, and <. 1072 churches, and '■ members; in Scotland, 216 church' members; in Ireland, 77 churches, and 1492 iii ambers; in Canada, 74,22') members; in the West Indies, 23,990 ; in Germany, &c, 19,393.

bar.c: BAR is any elongated piece of wood, metal, or other solid substance. In the iron manufacture, B. is a rod either round or square shafted. The round axe made by drawing the iron red-hot through a bore or hole in a plate, and the square ones by passing it likewise red-hot through a roller-mill between two rollers counter-grooved, with their triangular-grooved faces forming the square opening fur the passage of the iron. BaUway and knee iron are made in the same manner. See Iron Manufacture .

BAR, in Ilydrography, is a bank opposite the mouth of a river which obstructs or bars the entrance of vessels. The B. is formed where the rush of the stream is arrested by the water of the sea, as the mud and sand suspended in the river- water are thus allowed to be deposited. It is thus that deltas are formed at the mouths of rivers. The navigation of many streams (as the Danube) is kept open only by constant dredging or other artificial means.
BAR, in Music, is a line drawn across the stave, to divide the music into small portions of equal duration ; each of these small portions is itself called

BAR, or BARB, in Heraldry, one of those more important figures or charges in heraldry which are known as ordinaries. By the heralds of this country , the ordinaries, or, as, by way of eminence, they are called, the 'honourable ordinaries,' are commonly reckoned as ten in number, the sub-ord!- naries, or minor cl ous. The B., like the Fess (q. v.), is formed by two horizontal lines passing over the shield, but it differs Bar. from it in size, the fess occupying a third, the B. only a fifth part of the shield. There is this further difference between these two ordinaries, that the fess is confined to the centre, while the B. may be borne in several parts of the shield. There is a diminutive of the B. called the Closet, which is half a B. ; and ae;ain of the closet, called the Bamilet, which is half a closet, or the fourth part of a bar. — Bar-cemel i3 a double bar, from the French jumeau, f.jumelle, a twin.

BAR, in Law. This word has several legal meanings ; thus, it is the term used to signify an enclosure or fixed place in a court of justice where lawyers may plead, or perhaps more correctly, where they can address their advocacy on behalf of their clients. A veded-off space within the Houses of Parliament is similarly called the B. See Pleading. The dock, or enclosed space where persons accused of felonies and other offences stand or sit during their trial, is also called the B. ; hence the to sion, ' prisoner at the bar.' This word is likewise applied to the gate or rail thrown across a turnpike road for the levying of the toll-duties. It has also a general meaning in legal procedure, signifying something by way of stoppage or prevention . There is also a trial at B., that is, a trial before the judges of a particular court, who sit r for that purpose in banc (q. v.). See the following articles : Bar op Dower, Pleas in Bar, Trial at Bar, Tollbar, Felony, Treason, Barristers , Advocates. BAR OF DOWER. Dower, the estate or provision which, by the law of England, a widow is entitled to out of the lands and tenements of her deceased husband, may be barred or defeated by her elopement , her divorce on the ground of her own adultery , the treason of her husband, and other disabilities , and by detaining the title-deeds or evidences of the estate from the heir untd she restores them. A woman might also, while fines and recoveries were in force, be barred by these assurances, as she now may by the new method of conveyance appointed by the statute 3 and 4 Will. IV. c. 74, in substitution for a fine or recovery, in the case of a married woman. And another method of barring dower is by jointure, as retaliated by the statute 27 Henry VUI. c. 10.— Stephen's Commentaries, vol. L i See Dower, Jointi i:e. Widow, Fines and RECOVERIES , and COMMON AssUBANCt The term corresponding to Dower in Scotch law is Tbrcb (q. v.), which may also be barred or excluded in various ways ; as, for instance, by the widow's express discharge or renunciation, by the deeds of the husband affecting his real estate, by the husband's conviction for treason, by the wife's express acceptance of a different provision in lieu of the terce, and by her divorce on the ground of adultery.

Inside of the coral-reefs, the coast, excepting at two points, presents long lines of sandy beach — one of the most remarkable 6>0 y with iU expo I . I I ad, on occasional I of yellow fever, the climate is healthy. In 1844, the fall of rain was 72 inches; the temperature is said to have ranged only between ,<■, and 83.;" l\ shocks of earthy are sometimes felt, and thunder-storm quent and seven But hurricanes are the grand scourge of Barbadoea. In 1780, one of them destroyed 4326 persons, and property to the value of £1,320,664 .sterling; and in 1831, anotl; stroyed 1591 persons, and property to the value of £1,602,800 sterling. Of the former of these, the violence appears to have surpa ted all belief the winds and the waves between them having carried a 12-pounder gun a distance of 1 10 yards. In 1834, the commencement of the appn ship under the imperial act of emancipation, the population was 102,231 ; by 1861, it had inci to 152,727, being an average of 920 inhabitants to every square mile. The trade and the revenue bear a similar testimony to the benefits of emancipation. Between 1833 and 1870, the revenue had increased From 620,975 to £104,932; the imports from £481,610 to £1,069,868; the exports from £408,363 to £973,020; the total tonnage entered and cleared in 1x711 was 27S.517 tons. During that year, sugar was exported to the value of £594,690; 111. .lasses, valued at £98,383 ; and wheat, at £71,298. Being universally cultivated in regular plantations, the island affords no room for the squatting of negroes on unreclaimed lands, as in Jamaica and other West-India possessions . On this account, if from no "tier cause, the negro population have been compelled to labour diligently for hire, and are generally in a condition most creditable to their industry and prudence — contrasting , in this respect, with the improvidence and indolence of some of the lower classes among the whites. Altogether, however, the Barbadians are a shrewd and clever people, nor are they deficient in a due appreciation of their own power and importance, B. is the see of a bishop. It contains also many well-endowed seminaries — Codrington College, in p articular, having a revenue of £3000 a year. It was first colonised by the English in 1625, having previously been depopulated by the Spaniards.

barbara.c:
BA'RBARA, Saint, who suffered martyrdom at Nicomedia, in Bithynia, about 236, or, according to ..tier accounts, at Heliopolis, in Egypt, about 306, was of good birth, and well educated by her father, Dioscorus. To avoid disturbance in her studies, he had a tower built for her, where she spent her youth in the deepest solitude. While in this retirement, she was led, through Origen, as is said, to embrace < 'liiisl iauity. Her father, a fanatic heathen, learning his daughter's conversion, and failing to induce her to renounce Christ, delivered her up to the governor, Martianus, to be dealt with by the law. Martianus, struck with the intelligence and beauty of the maiden, attempted first by arguments to make her

relinquish Christianity, and when that failed, had recourse to the most exquisite tortures. A,1 the blinded father offered himself to strike i daughter's head. Scarcely w:l3 *^e deed done, when i struck with lightning. Hence St B. is to this day prayed to in storms. For the same reason, she is the patron saint of artillery, and her was at one time frequently placed on an powder-magazines, &c. The powder-room in a French ship of war is to this day called Sainte- Barbe. St B.'s day is the 4th December.

barbarian.c: BARBA'RIAN (Or. 6 among the Greeks, as early as the time (if Homer, signified one who could not speak the Greek language; and this restricted signification was not wholly obsolete even in the age of Plato, for the latter divides the entire human race into HeUenes and Barbaroi. The of the word is unknown, if it be not artificially formed, on the principle of imitation, to represent a meaningless babble of sound, such as the Greeks conceived all foreign languages to lie. It first began to acquire its secondary and invidious signification at the period of the Persian wars. The Greeks, who always exhibited a proud consciousness of their superior intellect and privileges, employed the term to designate the character of their enemies. It then meant whatever was opposed to G reek civilisation, freedom, or intelligence; but it coidd not yet have attained the degraded sense in which it is now used, for the Romans in the time of Plautus accepted the appellation, and called themselves Barbaroi. Subsequently, when Rome, under Augustus, became the mistress of the world, the word was applied to all the Germanic nod Scythian tribes with whom she came into contact. In modern times, B. signifies savage, uncivilised, or ignorant.

barbarossa.c: BARBARO'SSA, Aroodje or Harudj and Khaik EoDlN",two brothers, renegade Greeks, natives of Mitylene, who, as Turkish corsairs, were the torn >r of the Mediterranean during the first half of the 16th c. They made themselves masters of Algeria (q. v.) and Tunis, and brought these countries under the sovereignty of the Turkish sultan.

barbarotjx.c: BARBAROTJX, CHARLES, one of the most distinguished and energetic of the Girondists, was born at Marseille in 1767. The new ideas of equality and fraternity found in B. a warm advocate, and he did much to promote their spread. He was elected the special delegate of Marseille, to attend the Constituent Assembly at Paris. There he opposed the court, and took part with the minister, Roland, then out of favour. After the events of the 10th of August, he returned to his native town, where he was received with enthusiasm, and was soon after chosen delegate to the Convention. In the Convention , he adhered to the Girondi ts, and belonged to tie party who, at the trial of the king, voted for an appeal to the people. As li. boldly opposed the party of Marat and Robespierre, and even directly accused the latter of aiming at the dictatorship, he was, in May 1793, proscribed as a royalist and an enemy of the republic. He wand, red about the country, hiding himself as he best could, for thirteen months, when he w as taken, and perished at Bordeaux by the guillotine, June 25, 1794. 1$. understood the revolutionary or., is much better than the most of his party. Had the Girondists generally possessed anything like his energy iy. the Jacobins must have succumbed, and much oloo and horror would have been spared to Fran the world.

BA'RBARY, an extensive region in Northern Africa, comprising the countries known in modern 1 of Barca, Tripoli 1' Fezzan, Tuni i, Al the hall ofSus; and in ancient Africa • notes. It stretches from I to the Atlan' ad from the M to the 1 ' bara, or between long. 10" W. and •_'.".' I!., and lat. 25*- 37" N. The north-west of this region is divided by the Atlas Mountains into two parts: the northern comprising Marocco. ria, and Tunis ; the southern, a half-desert n called Belud ; pertaining geographically to Africa, B. is not specially African in an i racteristics ; but in climate, flora, fauna, and geological configuration, belongs to that great region which forms the basin of the Mediterranean. It is watered by many small streams, which either flow into the Mediterr or into the salt-lakes on the edge of the Desert, ling as tie y rise on the northern or southern slopes of the Atlas Mountains. A large port the country is capable of cultivation, and sandy or rocky tracts are rare, except on the southern m During the time3 of the Carthaginians, < Romans, it was richly fertile, and all the natural conditions of its ancient productiveness still remain. — For an account of the climate, geology, productions , &c, see the various com; Among the people, besides the French and other Europeans, seven distinct races may be enumerated : & rbers (or Kabyles), Moors, Beduins, Jews, Turks, sand Negroes. The Berbers and Beduins inhabit the open country, while the Moors, on tile other hand, reside in the towns. Most of the Berber tribes are either wholly free, or subject to the mere nominal jurisdiction of native chiefs, kaids, judges, &c. The Beduins luxuriate in equal liberty, had settled here in ancient times, but the greater number of that race immigrated when the Moors were expelled from Spain. The Turks entered B. in the 16th c. They form the dominant race in Tripoli and Tunis, but never establish d themselves permanently in Marocco. Their sway in Algeria was brought to an end by the French. The Kuluglis (the children of Turks by native mothers) are ex from the possession of all the paternal rights and privileges. The negroes are not natives of P.. but are brought I : I ives, principally from Sudan and Guinea. They are for the most part domestic slaves. The population, exclusive i t .less and Christians, is about 10,000,000, all Mohammed ana. Arabic is the language of commerce and inter, and in Marocco, the language of government, and the mother-tongue of Beduins, Moors, and i but in Tunis and Tripoli, where, as we have said, the Turks are still dominant, the language of government is Turkish. The Berbers Proper, or Kabyles, daily in the highlands, to which they have been driven by foreign conquerors, use a peculiar speech among themselves. In the oldest historical times, we find the Mauri (the ancestors of the modern Moors) mentioned as i in the north-west of B., the Numidians in the interior and eastern parts, and the Phoenician i on the coasts. These last people formed and founded cities— among them Ihppo, Hadrumi turn, ] about 1 B.O. It does not appear that they ever penetrated far into the interior. Confining themselves to the coast between the Great 5 and the Sb of ( ■ maintained com- with the people of ir and the seaports oi the Mediterranean. In the 7th c. B.C., the Greeks founded Cyrene, considerably to the i Carths ; I the plateau of Bama, now stvled Jebel-el-Achdar by the Arabs. 'While the J Ml

••s held sway on the coast, the Mauri and the Numidians wen divided into several indent tribes, and, like their neighbours the i. ware wholly uncivilised. Aft t the second Punic war, the Romans extended their sw.i i Carthaginian Africa, which became a Roman province at the close of the third I'unic war, wh D the city of Carthage was sacked and Numidia was 'annexed' alter the victory over ha, and Mauritania after the defeat 01 King the ally of Pompey's party. 'I h • s ■■ ■ ■ Julia. 1 ■ same name, was allowed I as a nomin l l bj nstos; but was. in fact, a Roman province. Thus, the ul a territory in Africa extending from t: -vrtis to the Atlantic (correspond in;.; to the modern states of B.), which formed si the largest and most flourishing provinces of their vast BB . crywhere they built large towns, ■whose extensive ruins are still to be seen scattered over the whole land, even to the verge of the 1 ; as. for instance, those at El-Haman, in the r ncy of Tunis, at Sava, Musulupium, and espe- the splendid city of ruins, Lambasa, not far from the Desert of Sahara. The Bomai in general, only two legions, numbering 24,000 men, in their African provinces; nevertheless, authority was uncontested, and they were enabled to undertake important works, such as the cistei i nets at Rusicada, Hippo, and Cirta, and the temples and amphitheatres of Calama and Annua, which clearly shew that the inhabitants enjoyed the benefits of a safe and powerful civilisation. Under Constantine, North Africa was divided into the several provinces, Mauritania-Tingitana, tania-Carsariensis (on the east of the former), Mauri- tania-Sitifensis, Numidia, Zeugitania, Byzacium, Cyrenaiea, and t rtica. At the di of the empire, tb . ith the tion of the last, fell to the share of the Western Empire. About this time, Christianity was promulgated in Africa, and with such success, that in the three Mauritanias there were more than iceses. As Roman power declined in Europe, ■nsequences were severely felt in the .' provinces. Religious disturbances, native revolts, the ambitious aspirations of the Roman governors after independence, loosened the political bands which bound the provinces together, and made them an easy prey to the Vandal I in Africa, in 420 A. P., under the ferocious Genseric, and in an incredibly short space of time overran the country, which they savagely missed in 1 1 i l 633, when they were defeated by Justinian's great general, Beusarms. Meai the Numidians and the Mauri had made them masters of the interior and of the coast of Maun Tingitana, and the Greek-Roman territories were restricted to the neighbourhood of Carthage and some points on the coast. The whole country of B. was thus made an easy prey for the Arabs, and in G47. Abdallah-bcn-Said, with 40,000 fanatical Mohammedans from Egypt, defeated and slew tile Greek prefect, Gregorius, at Tripoli. He did not. however, follow up his victories; but in G65 — 670 A.D., the Arabian general, Akbah, conquered the coast-towns of Tripoli, founded Cairo, and extended his sway almost to the Desert. Hassan, the get of the Calif Abd-el-Malek, in G92, stormed, plundered , and destroyed the new Carthage, and, in fact, annihilated the Greek-Roman dominion in In the course of less than a century, the part of the native tribes were converted forcibly to the faith of Islam. In 7S9, the western provinces separated themselves from the others, and Edris- ben-Abdallah founded there the dynasty of the After 800, ^ ben-Aglah, declared himself independent) and I the dynasty of the Aglabites, Afric i the califs. From this time down to i the changes of dynasty in R. were so frequent, that mot here describe them in detail. The results were, that independent states arose in Algeria, Oran, . Tenez, &c. About this time, also, began the I reaction of the Christian world against Mohamme- ! danism in North A Spain. St Louis undertook an expedition against Tunis. The Mom I by, expelled from Spain, and settled tbein- j selves on the coast of Northern Africa, there to that course of piracy by which they became . first as a fierce retaliation against Christian persecutors, but ultimately as a barbarous profession. As early as the time of Ferdinand the Catholic, the Spaniards sought to check their insolent ravages, and landed in Africa ral occasions, capturing the ports of Ceuta, Mclilla, Oran, Bugia, the island before Algiers, and Tripoli The Portuguese landed on the coast of Marocco, where at first they had great success ; but they were ultimately compelled to leave the country. ■ arious changes of fortune, Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli were brought under the government of the sultan. Since 1830, however, the first of these (see i.v) has been under French sway, while for i ears the other two have been only nominally hunt on the Turkish ruler. A similar fate, at a much earlier period, befell the western part of B., where the successors of the Arabian Sherif, Mula- Mehemed, overthrew the kings of Marocco and Fez, and established the Sherif dynasty, which rules to the present day over these lands.— Shaw's Travels and Observations relative to several Parts of B,; Mauroy, Du Commirce des Peuples de FAfri'jue nale (Par. 1845).

EA'RBARY APE, PIGMY APE, or MA'GOT, a small spec! or tailless monkey, interesting as the only one of the monkey race which is found in Europe. The only European locality, however, in which it occurs i . ■ of Gibraltar, and it is ■ have been originally brought from the north of Africa. It inhabits the precipitous sides of the Rock, inaccessible to human foot, and enjoys a certain ire of protection from firearms in return for the amusement afforded by its manners. It is gregarious , and large numbers are often seen together, the females carrying their young upon their backs. In some parts of the north of Africa, the B. A. is Barbarv Ape. extremely abundant, inhabiting rocky mountains and woods. It displays great agility in passing from tree to tree, and its bands often plunder gardens, one of their number keeping careful watch. It feeds on fruits, roots, &c. ; and its fondness for eggs is supposed to have given rise to the ancient story of

the battle of the pigmies and the cranes. It is of a greenish-gray colour, paler underneath ; and in size resenil ■ cat. The characters agr those of the genus llaeaau (Wanderoo Monkey, q. v., &c), except that the tail is reduced to a mere tuber, le. The mil bat elongated, although not nearly so much as in the baboons, with which this ape has sometimes been classed, and the facial angle is much higher than hi them. The face is almost naked. hat wrinkled. The ears are in form not unlike human ears. The eyes are round, reddish, and of great vivacity. The B. A. is one of keys most frequently to be seen in captivity, at least in Britain ; and possessing a considerable degree of intelligence, is capable of being trained to many tricks. In order to this, however, it must be taken young, as the older ones are often sullen and I My walks on four feet, although it can be trained to stand or walk, in a more awkward mamier, on two. It is filthy in its habits.
