bastards.c:
BA'STARDS and BASTARDY. Bastard described by Blackstone, are such children i i net born either in lawful wedlock, or within a competent time after its determination. The Scotch lawyers, again, true to their peculiar law of ma I bod as a child bom of a woman, who was not married to the father at the time of < tion, and who wa* , ,n. It was at one time the law of England, wh a mensa et thoro were adjudged by the < courts, that if the wife had children during the legal separation occasioned by the former kind of divorce, such chddren were pi bastards — for the law presumed the parties to live conformably to the sentence of separation. But in n times, the presumption has changed, and now always favours legitimacy. Bastards are incapable of ii i I i in 'perty ; nor can they claim any share of pi i <mial e tate as next of kin to a party dying intestate. They are said to be filii nonius, or viii pc ms of nobody, or the sons of the people, having no inheritable blood in them. As laid down, however, in many authorities, and among others in the last (4th) edition of Stephen - I here is an i tion to this ride in the case of a bastan 1 r puisne*, and where, it may be observed, the principle of the Scotch law of legitimation appears to some extent to be admitted. Thus, where a man has a bastard son, called a basfai (<J. v.), and afterwards marries the mother, and by her has a legitimate sou, who, in the language of the law, is ,11 1 : ,- I'ttisne — if the father dies, and the I fi'jni enters upon his laud, and enjoys it to his death, and dies seised thereof, whereby the inheritance descends to his issue, 1 1 and all other heirs are totally barred of their right, because the laws of England pay such a regard to a person in the situation of the bn.third eigne*, that after the land had descended to his would not unravel the matter again, and Buffer his estate to be shaken. But this indulgence was shewn to no other kind of bastard; for if tie mothi never married to the father, such bastard could have no colourable title at all. And the above exi would almost appear to be the law of England at the present day. But a recent statute renders this opinion somewhat doubtful, for by the 3 and 4 W ill. IV. c. 27, s. 39, it is enacted that no descent cast, after the 31st day of December 1833, shall defeat any right of entry or action for the recovery of land. By descent cast is meant an heir of a party who had com illegally to enjoy the land without challenge during his life, and was thereby enabled to transmit it to his heir, who thenceforward had a title which could

not be impeachi'il either by the original rightful owner, or by any of his descendants. The statute, however, has cut off the rights in this behalf of all such descents cast, and the true owner can now, under the pi E the act, always recover. But is the son of a fa cast' as is contemplated by the 3 and 4 Will. IV. c. 27? It may be doubted whether he is. The expression ut cast ' is generally applied in law-hooks to who, under a forcible, wrongful , and illegal entry on the land, bad - ■ ieded in diverting the inheritance from the direct and nal channel. But such i3 not the position of a tattard ■ ignt. Be is not, in any sense of the word, a stranger ; nor is the above privilege or favour allowed him and his family at all in respect of his position towards, or of anything that can be called his title to the /„„,/, but such privilege and favour are "is en him solely because of his peculiar bculardy. In tact, it is just because he is not astranger, but his father's eldest sou by birth, that the law from ancient times decided that he should not be altogether deprived of what otherwise would ha\ his natural rights. The rule, as we hav< appears to be founded on the principle of the Scotch law of subs lunation; and the intention probably was to give effect to the good feeling of the second or other legitimate son, who, from a regard to his mother's character, as well as his i position, might find himself excused from asserting his claims. Whether the above statute can. by its general terms, be understood arbitrarily to alter such a reasonable ami natural law of family 1 is a question for lawyers and law-courts. Tie- point, however, is important for popular explanation . In all other cases, the law of England appears to be as distinct as it is severe. It has even been decided that a child bum before wedlock in a foreign country, and according to whose law such child was legitimate, could not inherit land in England where his bastardy was indelible. There can be no collateral succession through bastards ; for as they cannot be heirs them SO neither can they have any heirs but those of their own bodies. A bastard is not entitled to the name either of his reputed father or of that of his mother, though he may acquire for himself a surname by tion ; nor can he take property by the mere I'tion of c/wild of his reputed parent, until he has acquired the reputation of standing in that relation to him. Nor does a bastard follow, as legitimate children do, his father's place of parochial settlement under the poor-laws, but he has and follows the settlement of his mother until he attain of 10, or until he acquires a mant in his own right, and after that age his primary settlement is in the parish where he was born. Another peculiarity of the status of bastardy is, that a bastard being ««, the consent of his father or mother to his mania and is of no avail ; but a guardian may be appointed by the ( oiirt of Chancery for the purpose, or a granted upon oath made that there is no person authorised to To this may be added, that although in general a may by deed or will appoint a guardian for his infant child, in the event of bis .1 has no such privilege if the child be illegitimate. .Such may be stated to be the principal peculiarities attaching to bastardy in the law of England. In other respects, a bastard is very much in the same position as a legitimate person. Thus, he can hold land in fee-simple, and can dispose of it as he may think proper, making an unlimited alienation of it ; and of course he can make a will bequeathing his whole estate ; a simple and reasonable privilege, 47 however, which, strange to say, was not conceded to bastards hi Scotland dying without lawful issue, till tie- year 1836, when an act of parliament was tie- 6 Will. IV. e. 22, which, on tl amble that ' it is just, humane, and expedient,' empowi Is in that country to dis|>o«e of their person I property by testament or will in like ergons might do, any law or practice to the contrary notwith In regard to his whole estate, although is entitled in the ease of a bastard dying intestal royal claim is not strictly enforced; but upon petition, rwn's right will "lie transferred to the nearest member of the deceased bastard's family. In the I Scotch law, also, the crown may, by what is a gift a/ bastardy, grant not only the personal, but the real estate of an intestate bastard to the ' donatory,' or person similarly entitled, as in the case i ty in England. It is also to be that the prohibitions as to marriage which extend to collaterals, and to those related by the half blood only, also apply although one of the parties be a bastard. Again, the laws relative to incest apply to a bastard with equal force as to others ; the principle of the two latter points l«ing that, although the bastard lje Jiliux nulliua as to many civil consequences, his relationship to his natural pan nt is recognised for moral purposes. Of course, it need not be added that a bastard may be made legitimate by an act of parliament for all a for that of inheriting land, ' as was done,' says Black-st' me, 'in the case • if J. >hn of Gauut's bastard children by a statute of Richard II.' The paternity of a bastard or illegitimate child in England is ascertained by several statutes — 7 and S Vict. c. 101, 35 and 36 Vict c. 65, 36 and :;7 Vict, c 9 ; and the father is bound to make a proper allowance for the child's support till sixteen. But it is on the mother herself that the maintenance of the child in the first instance devi 8 is for this purpose entitled to its custody in preference to its lather ; and she is bound to maintain it as part of her family while she remains unmarried, or until the child attains the age of 16, or gains a I ment in its own right, or (being a female) is married ; and in the event of the mother's marriage, the same liability attaches to her husband. If the mother be of sufficient ability to maintain the bastard, while he is so dependent on her, and neglect that duty, so that he becomes chargeal lie to a parish, she is liable, by 7 and S Vict. c. Ml, s. 6, to be punished under the provisions of the (q. v.). Whether the mother b of sufficient ability or not, she can, by affiliation proceedings, compel the father to pay a sum not exceeding five shillings a week till the child is sixteen (35 and 36 Vict 0. 68 t s in the Scotch law to which we have adverted, it is to be observed that in that i. the maintenance, or ' aliment,' as it is called, of illegitimate children, is a joint burden upin both parents. Tie mother is entitled to the custody of the child, but it does not appear whether she is to have such custody for any fixed time. It is in the discretion of the Court of S to deb nnine this, and it would seem that the period may vary according to circumstances, from seven to fourteen years. During this tune, the father is bound to contribute his proportion of the expense; and if neither the father nor mother can support the child, it must be maintain, d by the parish in which the mother has a settlement. There is a nice and curious difference in the laws of England and Scotland as to the mode of ascertaining the paternity of a bastard child. According to the statutes we have referred to, that fact may W

be proved in England l>y the evidence of the mother, provided her statement is supported m 'some material particular' by other testimony. But in Scotland, the order of the inquiry is reversed; the woman's evidence in that country being taken :;]d only where the other and indepi evidence amounts to what is called a em/ lire as induces a i lief, although not complete evidence, in which case she is admitted to give what is called hi in supplement. Both in England and Scotland, the widow of a bastard, whether there be issue or not of the marriage, is entitled to dower, teres, jus relictce, and all the othi ■ [hts of widows. The 'defender,' or person against whom ; nit is formally brought, is the party who would have succeeded to the bastard, had he been legitimate , 1!. can also be judicially dec! similar mode of proceeding at the suit of a party who lias any other interest, or, indeed, any interest , to have such illegitimacy determined. bastia.c: BASTI'A, the former capital of Corsica, is picturesquely situated on the slojie of a mountain, rising from the sea in the form of an amphitheatre, in the north-eastern part of the island, in lat. 42" 42' N., and long. 9° 27' E. It has about 20,000 inhabitants. The streets are narrow and crooked. It has a harbour suitable for small vessels, defended by a mole, at the mouth of which is a rock resembling a lion couchant, and designated ' II Leone.' There is a considerable trade in leather, skins, wine, oil, figs, and pulse ; and many stilettos and daggers are manufactured here, which are prim exported to Italy. Until recently, the printing- presses of B. were actively employed in the production of Italian publications that would not have been permitted to appear in that country itself. B. was founded in 1380 by the Genoese Leonel Lomellino. During last century, it was oftener than once taken by the British. It was made, in 1791, the capital of the French department of Corsica, which rank was afterwards transferred to Ajaccio. It is the scat of the highest courts of the island.

bastiat.c: BASTIAT, Frederic, an eminent political economist, was born at Bayonne on the 29th of June 1S01. His father was a merchant, and educated his son with a view to the same profession. After completing his studies, B. entered the commercial house of one of his uncles, established at Bayonne, and employed his leisure hours in the study of political economy. Circumstances called him into Spain and Portugal in 1S40, where he took advantage of the opportunity afforded him to study the customs and institutions of these two countries, which have still much to learn before they can be on a footing of equality with other nations in 733 matters of finance and political economy. His first appearance as an author was in 1844, when he published , in the Journal tlt.i Ecu* article ' I 'u uenoe of French and English Tariffs on the tive Futures of the two Peoples.' Itcontained i l'..'s theory of political economy, who, from i di cide I opponent ol of protection. Subsequently, in the same journal, he combated the economic fallacies of Socialism and the rights of labour. During a \ i.-it to England, he made the acquaintance of Cobden, and on his return to France, he translated (1845) the Bpe of the free-traders, which he published With an Lctory preface, entitled Cobden and or the English Agitation in Favour of Fi which he gathered up into one solid mass the incon- iea of the protective system. I'., now went e in 1'aris, where he continued to props his views with considerable success; I ry of the societies, and chief editor of the journal, established to vindicate the princip! free trade. After the revolution of 1848, lie was i successively a member of the Constituent and Legislative assemblies. In 1S50, he can ward as the ist of the Socialist writer, Prudhon. Suffering from pulmonary di . I a repaired to Italy for change of climate, but died at Borne on the 24th December 1850. des the writings mentioned, B. pub Sopliismes Economiques — Propriiti it Lot, Ju Fraternili — Protectionisme et Communisms, Harmonies . Economiques, and several other important tractates, all of which cxliibit extensive known I the subjects discussed, convincing logic, and a | of sprightly and biting satire. The Sars Economigues has been translated into English by P. J. Stirling {Harmonies <y Inn-ay, Lond. 18G0). The soundness of the principles which the writings of B. uphold, notwithstanding the pro. tectionist tendencies of the late president, M. Thiers, i now (ls7i!i generally acknowledged in France.

bastile.c: BASTIDE, Jul i 1 I i i ich journalist and politician . Minister of Foreign Affairs in 1848, and mi of the Constituent Assembly, was born at Paris in 1800. In 1S21, he became one of the first members of the French Carbonari ; and after the July revolution , he was conspicuous among the writers of the radical opposition. On the reconstitution of the National Guard, B. was elected commandant- in-ehief of the legion of artillery, in which the republicans were grouped, and took part in two insurrectionary movements, for the second of which — the (meule at Paris, 5th June 1832— he was condemned to death, but escaped to London. Pardoned in 1834, he returned to Paris, and again devoted himself to politics in the columns of the National. 1!.. however, being one of those Nco-catholic republicans who regarded the Church of Rome as the religious synonym of democracy, could not heartily sympathise with the tone of that newspaper on religious topics, and in 1847 he founded the J' we tTationaie, in which he advocated his peculiar opinions. During the revolution of 1848, he was a Supporter of General Cavai'jnae, and an opponent of Socialism. In 1858, he published//'; RtpubHoue ' Vltalie en 1848 ; and in 1859, Guerres de Religion en France.

bastille.c:
BA'STILLE was, in France, a general term for a strong fortress, defended by towers or bastions (q. v.), and in this sense it was used in England also after the Norman Conquest. The famous prison to which the name latterly was appropriated, was originally the castle of Paris, and was built by order of Charles V., between 1370 and 13S3, by Hugo Aubriot, Prfivdt or Provost of Paris, at the

Porte St Antoine, as a defence against the English. Afterwards, when it came to be used as a state- prison, it was provided, during the 16th and 17th centuries, with vast bulwarks and ditches. On each of its longer sides the B. had four towers, of five 6toric3 each, over which there ran a gallery, which was armed with cannon. It was partly in these towers, and partly in cellars under the level of the ground, that the prisons were situated. The unfortunate inmates of these abodes were so effectually removed from the world without as often to be entirely forgotten, and in some cases it was found impossible to discover either their origin or the cause of their incarceration. The B. was capable The Bastille. of containing 70 to SO prisoners, a number frequently reached daring the reigns of Louis XIV. and Louis XV. Though small compared to the number which an ordinary prison contains, these numbers were considerable, when we reflect that they rarely consisted of persons of the lower ranks, or such as were guilty of actual crimes, but of those who were sacrificed to political despotism, court intrigue, ecclesiastical tyranny, or had fallen victims to family quarrels — and were lodged lure in virtue of letlres de cachet (q. v.) — noblemen, authors, savans, priests, and publishers. On the 14th of July 17S9, the fortress was surrounded by au armed mob, which the reactionary policy of the court had driven into fury, and to the number of which moment added The garrison consisted of 82 invalids and .'!_' Swiss. The negotiations which were entered into with the governor led to no other result than the removal of the cannon | on the Faubourg St Antoine, which by no means contented the exasperated multitude. Some cut the chain3 of the first drawbridge, and a contest took place, in which one of the besieged and ISO of the people were killed, or severely WOW but the arrival of a portion of the troops which had already joined the people with four field-, turned the fortune of the conflict in favour of the besiegers. Delaunay, the governor — who had been ited by one of his officers, when on the point of blowing the fortress into the air — permitted the second drawbridge to be lowered, and the people rushed in, lulling Delaunay himself and several of his officers. The destruction of the B. commenced on the following day. amid the thunder of cannon, and the pealing of the Te Deum. This event, in itself apparently of no great moment, leading only to the release of three unknown prisoners — one of whom had been its tenant for thirty years— and four forgcrs, and in which it is said only the 664 persons whose names now appear on the column in the Place de la Bastille, took part, nevertheless finally broke the spirit of the court-party, and changed the current of events in France.

bastinado.c: BASTINADO (from the Fr. boston or baton, a cudgel), the name given by Europeans to the punishment in use over the whole East, which consists in blows with a stick, generally upon the soles of the feet, but sometimes upon the back.

bastion.c: BA'STION, in Fortification, is one of the principal defence-works in a fortified place. It is a kind of tower, very broad in relation to it3 height, The plain wall, called the curtain, which often surrounds a fortified town, is usually a polygon of many sides ; and in that case, bastions occupy all, or nearly all, the salient angles. Bastions are mostly five- the two outermost sides are theyiices, meeting in an angle towards the enemy ; the two on either side of these are the Jlanks, meeting two curtains or portions of wall; and the fifth side, open to the interior of the fortified place, is the gorge. Bastions may be regarded as projections, which enable the defenders to watch the approach of the enemy to the foot of the wall, and to frustrate them by a Hanking fire. Taking the average range of modern ordnance and muskets as a basis, engineers decide on a distance of 300 to 400 yards between B. and B. ; but if Armstrong or Napoleon guns, and Enfield or Minie rifles, should hereafter be employed in attacking and defending fortified places, these figures will probably need modification. The length of each face and flank of a B. is so regulated, that two bastions can defend each other and the intermediate portion of wall. This principle was partly acted upon in the middle ages; but some of the Italian military engineers of the 16th c. first constructed the B. proper. The main substance of a B. is an immense mound of earth, capable of supporting heavy guns, and of receiving the fire of the enemy ; but it is faced and strengthened in many parts with brick and stone. The top is broad enough to allow room for the large guns, and for infantry ami artillery soldiers. A hollow B. has the space within it kept down to the level of the town or natural ground; but a solid B., tilled up to the top with firm materials, is considered to be the best defensive construction. Vauban, the great French en. devised the plan of having large turns opposite the chief angles of the place, with a ditch behind each ; a tower or small B. being placed at the real angle of the wall behind. This was intended to enable the besieged to hold out for some time, even after the great bastions were taken. The relation wdiich bastions bear to the general system of attack and defence, is noticed under Fortification and Sieof. ; while various details on the subject will be found under Battery, < ' ISB- mate, CURTAIN, Dnvn, 1 iu BB \>; 1:1. K-.Ai.r, Para- li. I', Hamfart, &c. In wood-cuts illustrating many of these articles, the relative position of the I!, will be better shewn than by any diagram in this place.

basyle.c: BA'SYLE is the name given by chemists to a .simple or compound substance which can unite with oxygen to produce a base (q. v.). Thus, all the metals are examples of simple basvles. and ammonium (XII,), ethyle (C.1I ). methyle (C 11 I. ,'.r.. r. pp sent compound basylee. Another property which a B. possesses is, that it can unite with a salt radical (a. v.), like chlorine or cyanogen, to form salts. Thus, the B. sodium (Xa) combines with chlorine to produce a salt — in fact, common salt (NaC'l); and mercury (Hg) unites with cyanogen (Gy) to form the salt cyanide of mercury (Hg<

BAT, the common name of all animals of the class M ned with true wings, and so are capable of really living or propelling themselves in the air. They were all included by Linnaeus in the genus Vtspertilio (old Latin name), now subdivided and forming the family 739

VespertQionideB, which is very generally ri as of precisely i I at with the sub-order I optsrafGr. hand-winged), although tome naturalists still follow Cuvier in the Oaieo pUheada [Colugos or Flying Lemurs) as another Long-eared Bat [Plccottis auritus). Family of Cheiroptera. But besides other characters which connect the Colugos with Lemurs rather than with bats, they greatly differ from bats in having a mere I on of the skin of the Hanks attached to the limbs— as in the Flying Squirrels and Petaurists or Flying Phalangers, and in the Flying in among saurian reptiles — capable of sustaining them in the air like a parachute in a very extended leap, but not of being expanded and by a succession of strokes tor true Sight. The power of true flight, bats, on the contrary, possess; and some of them not only fly rapidly, Dul about very nimbly in the air, in pursuit of their insect prey. It is very interesting to compare the organs of flight in bats with those of birds, both as to the points in which they agree, and those in which they differ. They beat the air, as birds do, with ii anterior members ; but the requisite extension of surface is not obtained by quills, but by a lion of the arms and fingers, upon which a thin membrane is stretched, folding close to the body by moan; of their j lints, when the wing is not in use. A little attention to the aecoi figures of the skeleton of a bat and of a ba1 wdl make plainer than mere words can the relation of the bones of a bat's wing to the bones of the human arm and hand, or to the ordinary hones of the anterior extremities in quadrupeds which have or toes. The thumb, a (in figure of skel is .-lent, armed with a strong nail, and not at all included in the wing-membrane, nor used in flight. Skeleton of Bat. The bones most elongated of all arc the metacarpal bones, or bones of the hand, 4; the true finger-bones, r, are not so much so. The fore-arm, </, lie not two id ulna), but only one Olio ulna), with a sort of rudiment of the other; tie- rotatory motion, of which these two bones afford the means, being not only umn > my to bats, but at variance with tin- put I in this part of truetnio.iii a powerful stroke in particular direction. For a similar reason, 'the fingers of this strange hand are incapable of closing towards the I !mi, as ours do, when grasping an object: their only movements are SUCh as fold up tin t the side of the body, by Laying the fingers close along the side of the fore-arm, as in dosing a fan.' ( Ireat bren bh, however, n u i n qui be in the shoulder; and, accordingly, we find an anal birds in the size and solidity of the bones in this part, as well as in the thickness of tin- muscles by which the wings are moved, and still more in the great dimensions of the sternum, or breast-bone, to which they are attached. The sternum is also furnished with a medial ridge, as in birds, for the better attachment of the muscles. The ribs are large; but the other bones generally, as the the head and of the pelvis, are deli ate, and appear designed for lightness.— The wing-membrane of bats extends along the Hanks to the hind although these aid little in flight ; but it is attached to them so as to leave the feet free, which are much like the feet of ordinary small quadrupeds with toes and claws, and are employed along with tile thumbs of the anterior limbs in creeping upon the ground, in climbing perpendicular rough surfaces, or for Si i. Bat in repose. Dg with the brad downward in that remark- 0 lure of repose in which bats pass great part of their lives, and in which they differ from all Of hi r animals. In the greater number of species of B., the wing- membrane extends not only to the hind-legs, but beyond them to the tad, which is included in it, a l< culiar bone (e in fig. of skeleton) also arising from each heel to afford further support to this part of it, which seems to serve purposes analogous to the tail of birds, acting as a rudder, and enabling the animal to make those rapid evolutions in the air, which it is so pleasing to see as bats Hit about in the summer evening. The fruit-eating bats of tropical regions, which have no need to perform such evolutions, are destitute of this interfemoral part of the membrane ; and according to the habits for which each species has been designed, the tails are long or short, entirely included in the membrane, or oidy for part of their length, or produced a very little beyond it, and terminating in a hard tip, so that the tail is capable of being used to aid in creeping or climbing, evidently possessing considerable power, and being curved and moved in a

manner which suggests a slight analogy to the prehensile tails of monkeys. Bats were placed by Linnajus in his order Primates, along with monkeys and lemurs, with which they agree in their pectoral teats and in other characters, particularly of the organs of reproduction. In one genua (Dysopu*), there is an additional resemblance to the Primates in the partially opposable thumbs of the hind-feet, and a trace of this character is to bo found in the fore- thumbs, already noticed. Hats are now, however, generally placed by naturalists in the order Feree or Oarnana, although, like many other animals of that tn-eat order, most of them are by no means exclusively carnivorous. The greater part of them feed chiefly on insects, some chiefly on fruits. They exhibit considerable variety both in the number and character of their teeth, as might be expected in animal-; which differ so much in their food. All of them have four rather large canine teeth ; the incisors vary much in size and form, as well as in number. The digestive apparatus exhibits a variety corresponding with that of the teeth; the intestinal canal of the Vampyres (q. v.), which live by Backing the blood of animals, proceeding almost in a straight line from one extremity of the body to the other, whilst that of some of the Head of Pteropus. frngivorous bats, as the Kalong (i|.v.) (Pteropus) of Java, is seven times as lone as the body. Except in the power of Bight and things essential to it, bats present no resemblance to birds. The old English name VUttermouae, and the German Fledermaua, indicate an early popular recognition of their true place in creation. They are generally nocturnal animals, or, at least, prefer the twilight, although one of the British species may occasionally be seen pursuing insects during winter at mid-day. They generally spend the day in eaves, hollow tn i s, and oilier dark recesses, often under roofs of houses, and in crannies of ruined or deserted buildings. They are found in almost all parts of the world, except the very coldest, but are most numerous and of greatest size within the tropica Those of temperate climates generally spend the winter in a state of torpidity, in which, although circulation continues very languidly, respiration does not ordinarily take place. Tlie whole number known to Linnaeus amounted to a very few sjieeies. not half so many as are now known to inhabit Great Britain alone. Upwards of 130 species have been described, and there is great probability that the actual number existing is very much greater. It is not unlikely that Bom rated accounts of the great bats of warm cl ■•■ ive rise to the fable of the Harpies, which Virgil introduced into the .Km id The bats of Europe are all small ; the body of the largest British one is not so large as ;i mouse, and the fullest stretch of its wings about 15 inches, whilst the common British species are much smaller ; but in the Kaloug, already mentioned, the stretch of wing is 5 feet. Of ] species, the largest is the Noctule B. ( Vt ■-,.■ noctuld), a very local species, found chiefly in the south of England ; the 1 ' rdlus) is perhaps the most common. It was long confounded by British naturalists with the common B. of the continent of Eir |, which is much larger, and very rare in Britain. In some parts of the country, the Long-oared B. (PUcolvs Ot is very common. It U distinguished by its enormously large and very beautiful ears, which, when it is asleep, are folded up in a remarkable manner under the arm, the long tragus then resembling a slender 1 « Great Eat or Noctule Bat (J- 6 Greater Horseshoe Liat [B Both Uritish. ■rtnlti). cquinum). ear. This great development of the ears is characteristic of certain genera of I!., that part of the ear called the tragus attaining also a remarkable size, so that it seems like a smaller ear in front of each large one. In many species, only two of which are in Britain, there is a still more remarkable membranous or leaf-like appendage on the nose, which in some is simple, in some, complex, and often of large size, giving an extraordinary appearance to the face. Some o) the larger species, having a n I crest, are called Spectre lUts (q. v.). Only two species of B. (/.'/ ,r such an appendage, are found in Britain, both of tin in very rare; from the form which it assumes, they are called Horseshoe Bats. It is supposed that this nasal append is of use as a very delicate organ of touch, perhaps also of smell ; as the great ears may bo of use both for touch and hearing. These . must often guide bats when that of sight cannot be employed; and the sense of touch appears to be possessed in no ordinary degree even by the wing membrane. By supposing it to be affect- I by tin- pulsations of the air. i luvier accounted for the power displayed by bats which had been cruelly deprived of sight, of avoiding obje I which they flew, without the necessity of ascribing to them, as Spallanzani had done, the possession of a sixth sense. It deserves to be here noticed that, amongst the peculiarities which distinguish certain genera of bats, is the absence not only of the upper cutting teeth in the East Indian and African genus Megar derma, but even of the bone in which the -v teeth are usually placed ; and that another tropica] c , (, oi whii U the i found in Africa and .lava, have the skin attached to t he body only at a few points, and capable of being blown op like a bladder, at tile pleasure of the animal, by means which is inhaled through the nostrils into cheek-pouches communicating by small apertures with the gem ral .-kin-bag. The use of this is wholly unknown. Bats walk or creep awkwardly upon I one si.le of the body being jerked forward, and then the other, yet they run with considerable celerity. There is a common notion, that they cannot rise easily from a level surface, but must find eminence from which to throw themselves. Of tho fallacy of this, any one will soon be convinced

who gets a B. and places it upon the floor. — Bats commonly produce one or two young at a birth. — Bat walking (Plccotus aurilus). .Some of the species are very gregarious ; others often fly about in pairs ; great numbers, and of different species, are often found congregated in their places of hybernation or repose. — Some of the species are easily tamed, and become very familiar; but their odour is disagreeable, and it is generally found difficult to keep them long alive. Fossil remains of Cheiroptera are occasionally found in eocene rocks, but owing to the delicacy of the bones, great difficulty has been experienced in the determination of the genera and species.

BAT, or BAT (Fr.), in military matters, was originally the name of a kind of pack-saddle ; and hence a bat-horse was a baggage-horse bearing a bat or pack, and a bat-man was a servant in charge of the horse and bat. By a modification of meaning, a bat-man is now any soldier allowed to act as servant to an officer. When British troops arc sent on foreign service, bat-horses or mules are provided (if cai are not forthcoming) for carrying the regimental books, the kettles and tents, the medicine-chest, the veterinary medicine-chest, intrenching tools, armourers' stores, saddlers' stores, &c— about 20 such horses or nrules to each battalion. Bat-horses and bat-men are also provided for carrying officers' camp-equipage. An allowance for procuring these accommodations is usually called Bat-money.

batangas.c: BATA'NGAS, a seaport town of the Philippines, island of Luzon, and capital of the province of the same name. Lat. 13° 45' N., long. 121° 5' E. Distance from Manilla, oil miles S.; founded 1581. Top. of town and district, 17,000. B., which is well built, and has an elegant appearance, is likely situated on an extensive bay which opens into the Strait of Mindoro. Considerable advantage is taken of its facilities for commerce.

batardeau.c: BATARDEAU', a strong wall of masonry, built across the outer ditch of a fortress, to sustain the pressure of water when one part of the ditch is dry and the rest wet. It is built up to an angle at the top, and is armed with spikes, to prevent the enemy from crossing ; and sometimes a stone tower is provided to strengthen the defence. There is a sluice-gate to regulate the admission of water.

batatas.c: BATA'TAS, or SWEET POTATO (Convolvulus Batatas, or Batatas cdulis, the genus Batatas having recently been separated from Convolvulus [q. v. |, chiefly upon account of the four-celled ovary), a perennial plant with long creeping stems, heart-shaped leaves on long stalks, and variously lobed, large purple flowers much resembling those of the best known species of Convolvulus, and very large oblong acuminated tubers. It is a native of the East Indies, but is now cultivated in all tropical and subtropical countries for its tubers, which are highly esteemed as an article of food, and are eaten either roasted or boiled ; they are sweet, wholesome, and nutritious, but somewhat laxative. The B. forms, next to maize, the principal food of the poorer classes in some parts of America. Its cultivation is very easy ; it is readily propagated by tubers or by cuttings of the sb 111, requires little attention, and soon produces its tubers. In hot-houses in Britain, these are without difficulty obtained of 1 lb. or '2 lbs. '. The cultivation of the B. has been hit 10. d I into the south of Europe. In America, it is little cultivated to the north of New Jersey, and .<" there is inferior. The leaves are used as a boiled vegetable, It is the 1!., or sweet potato, which is usually meant by the older English write r . when they mention potatoes. Its tubers were imported into England by way of Slain, and BO a delicacy, before the potato was known. — Batatas panlculata, or Convolvulus paniculatus, a nearly allied Batatas. species, is cultivated in the same way as the common B., and its tubers are similar in quality. — To the new genus Batatas, has been referred also the plant formerly known as Ipomoea macrorhiza, now Batatas jalapa, so called from supposed purgative qualities of the root, which, however, it is found not to possess, being white, insipid, saccharine, and Farinaceous , and of great size, 50—60 lbs. in weight. The plant inhabits sandy soils in Georgia and Carolina.

batavi.c: BATA'VI (or, according to some MBS., Yatavi), the name of a German people, who anciently inhabited a part of the present Holland, particularly the island which was called after them, Batavia, fori 1 by the branch of the Rhine which falls into the sea at Leyden, the Waal, and the Mense. Their country, however, extended across the Waal, but its boundaries cannot now be precisely determined . According to Tacitus, they were originally a branch of the Chatti, who emigrated across the Rhine. They were conquered by Germanicus; became subject to the Romans, and served them so well, that they obtained the honorary title of friends and brothers of the Roman people ; were exempted from taxes and assessments, being only required to provide a proportion" of troops ; and were permitted to choose their commanders from amongst themselves. Their cavalry were particularly good, and were often employed by the Romans. The first who terms the insidar district inhabited by these Gauls, Batavia. is Zosimus, who also informs us that in the time of Constantius (358 A. v.) it had fallen into the hands of the Salii, a Frankish tribe.

batavia.c: BATA'VIA, properly the name of the island occupied by the ancient Batavi, became at a later date the Latin name for Holland and the whole kingdom of the Netherlands. The name Batavian IlEi'Ulsi.in was given to the Neth m their new organisation of ICtli May 1795, and they continued to bear it till they were converted into the kingdom of Holland, under Loui3 Bonaparte, 5th June 180G.

BATA'VIA, the capital of the empire of the Netherlands in the East Indies, stands on the north-west coast of .lava, at the mouth of the Tjili- wong, frequently called the Jaccatra, from the for- itive town, on the ruins of which the present city was built. There is good anchorage for large ships in the offing, ami it is navigable for smaller v els towards the interior. The influence of a vertical son on this Holland in miniature led it to become proverbial as the grave of Europeans. Latterly , however, the climate has been greatly unproved by draining. The temperature, though not extreme, is oppressive from its uniformity, the mean of winter being 7ST° F., and that of summer only 78-G°. The latitude is G° 7' 40" S., and the longitude 100° 62 E. Pop. 55,000. Notwithstanding the growing prosperity of Singapore, I!. continues to be the commercial emporium of the far East. Its markets present at once all the productions of Asia, and all the manufactures of Europe. In 1811, while Holland was a vassal of France, B. fell into the hands of the English, by whom it was restored to its former owners in 1816. Latterly, B. has found Singapore a formidable competitor for the trade between East and West. The Dutch government has recently laid a telegraphic cable along a line of COO mdes from B. to Singapore . The province of Batavia is low, but rises gently towards the south. The forests have all been cut down for the use of the sugar factories. It is well adapted for fruit-trees and vegetables, which are cultivated by Chinese gardeners. Pop. 401,563, eon- aisting of 4145 Europeans, 41,137 Chinese, 355,338 natives, and 943 foreign orientals. The peculiar character of the people has been lost by the influx of and intermarriage with strangers from all districts of the Indian archipelago. The language is a mixture of Soudanese, Malay, and other tongues, and is called low Malay. The largest estates are held by Europeans, the smaller by Chinese and natives. The religion is chiefly Mohammedan. There are goo. I post-roads. The industries continue to increase, and chiefly consist of factories for making machinery for distilling and for sugar works; distilling arrack, copper and tin work, dyeing, jfce. The nutmeg, cacao, and cocoa-nut tree are successfully grown.

batenburg.c: BA'TENBURG, a town of the Netherlands, in the province of Gelderland, situated on the right bank of the Maese, 9 miles west of Nymegen. It is worthy of notice only on account of its association with the Romans, whose Oppidv/m Balavorum it was. P..VTH, the chief city in Somersetshire, England, is beautifully situated in a wooded valley in the north-east part of the county, on the Avon, 20 miles from its mouth, ami 106 miles west of London. The 1 see are built wholly of white freestone — 'Bath oolite,' worked in the neighbouring quarries- being entirely discarded! The city has a liner appearance than any other in England, the variety of level giving very commanding sites for its tine and regular streets, crescents, and public buildings. The beauty and sheltered character of its situation , the mildness of its climate, and especially the curative efficacy of its hot chalybeate springs, have long rendered 15. a favourite fashionable re3ort. The springs, which are four in number, were known to the Romans, who bruit baths on the spot in the 1st c, of which extensive remains were discovered in 1775. The temperature of the springs varies from 97° to 117' P. ; they rise near the river bank, in the centre of the city, and discharge 184,320 gallons of water daily. The water is most useful in b nervous, and scrofulous complaints, palsy, rheumatism , gout, and cutaneous diseases. Though the gaiety of B. has greatly . days of the Prince Regent, there has been a great general improvement in the city, but the population somewhat diminished during the twenty years 1851 - 1871. It has two parks, and many public walk I open places ; theatre, concert-rooms, and other places of amusement ; subscription library, me club-house, educational institutions, &c. The Church is a cruciform structure in the latest p dicnlar style, with a line roof in the style of Henry VII.'s chapel, and a central tower 150 feet high. About a mile to the north-west is Beckford's Tower, built by the eccentric author of VaOuHc, bat now a cemetery chapel It is 154 feet high. B. returns two members to parliament. Pop. 53,704, at tines much increased by visitors. B. has no m of any note. Coal is found in the tirhood. The Great Western Railway from London to the west passes through the city. B. is oi quity ; it was a Soman station called : at the intersection of the great Roman ways from London to Wales, and from Lincoln to the south coast of England. Kichard I. granted 1!. it - extant charter, which was subsequently com by Henry III., and tended by George III. A greater number of Etonian remains havi found in and near B. than elsewhere in Britain ; they form a collection unrivalled in extent and value.

bath.c:
BATH, KNIGHTS of THE. The name of this order is derived from the ceremony of bathing, which used to be practised at the inauguration of a knight, as an emblem of the purity henceforth required of hiin by the laws of chivalry. The Collar and Cadge of the Lath. ceremony is of unknown antiquity, and is spoken of by writers of the 13th c. as an ancient custom. See Knight. The earliest authentic instai its observance which we have in this country, is in the time of Henry IV., who, in preparing for his coronation, made forty-six knights at the Tower of Loudou, who had watched all the night before, aud

bathed themselves. The last knights of the B. created in the ancient form were at the coronation of Charles II. in 1661. Front that period till the accession of the House of Hanover, the order I U into oblivion. It was revived by George 1. in 1725, and ia now the second order in rank in England, the Gist being the Garter. By the statutes then En '1 for the government of the order, it was declared that, besides the sovereign, a prince of Star of the Bath. the blood, and a great master, there should lie thirty -live knights. At the conclusion of the great -war, it was thought expedient, with a view to rewarding the merits of many distdngi officers, both military and naval, to extend the limits of the order, which was effected on the 2d January lSl.r>. But the order was still purely military, and it was not till 1847 that it was placed on its present footing by the admission of civil knights, commanders, ami companions. The following is its present organisation. First Class.— Knights Grand Cross (K.G.C.) ; the number not to exceed, for the military service, .riO, exclusive of the royal family and foreigners; and for the civil service. 25. Second Class.— Knights Commanders (K.C.B.); military. 102. and civil, .r>0, exclusive of Eon These, like the first, have the title Sir, and take precedence of Knights Bachelors. Third Class. — Companions (O.B.); military, 525, and civil, 200. They take precedence of Esquires, but are not entitled to the distinctive appellation of knighthood. No officer can be nominated to the military division of this class unless his name lias been mentioned in the London Gazette for di languished services in action; and the order has never been conferred on an officer below the rank of a major, or commander in the navy.

BATH, BATHING. By bathing is usually understood the immersion of the body, or a part of it, in water. In a more extended signification, it means the surrounding of the body with any medium differing in nature or temperature from its usual medium; thus, we speak of a blood-bath, a vapour- bath, a cold-air bath, a compressed-air bath (q.v.), an earth-bath. A fourfold division may be made of baths: 1. According to the substance with w bich the body is surrounded — into water, oil, milk, gas, .sand, and other baths ; 2. According to the manner of application — into river, slipper, plunge, shower, dropping, vapour, and douche baths; 3. According to the parts of the body subjected to the application —into whole, half, sitz, foot, hand, and eye ball.s; and 4. According to the temperature of the substance applied— into cold, tepid, warm, and hot baths. The practice of bathing undoubtedly reaches back earliest tunes in the existence of the human and Hi'1 most ancient historical accounts as well as popular myths make mention of it. Among the Egyptians, the bath was practised as a religious lit'1 ; and, in general, we find t! pinion prevailing throughout antiquity, that purification of the induced or signified ral purity. Man, it was thought, ought to present himself pure in body and Mini, when he engaged in the service of his god, or many transaction that brought him into immedi- ntact with that being. In making the bath a religious ordinance, Moses may have bad in view tlio prevention or more speedy cure of those skin-diseases so prevalent in the East The Mosaic Law prescribes expressly, in some cases, the use of running water, which has given rise, through a ■lii'standing, to the deleterious cellar-baths of the Jews. In Palestine, the wealthier Jew had 1'iu.ite baths in their houses, and ponds in their is, an arrangement which prevailed in all the civilised parts of the East, and which does so still. There were, besides, public bath-houses among the .less, as among other nations. Among the Greeks, also, bathing was very early in use. The practice is often alluded to in Homer. Bathing, among the Greeks, as among other nations, was counted a religious rite, and was connected with the preparations for sacrifice, for the reception of orach marriage, &e. Wc possess, however, no detailed accounts of the construction and arrangements either of private or of public baths in Greece, which last were mostly connected with the gymnasia. The men bat lied together; that there were public baths for women, appears probable from various iiulica- Among the Romans, although warm-baths [thermce) were in use from the earliest times, yet it was only at a late period that they were so extensively adopted ; and then the increase and nun I 1 spread of luxury had driven the primitive .object of bathing into the background, so that the public baths were looked upon as places of g. in ral n u-t f"i pleasure. The most of these public baths were built under the emperors. They were numerous in Rome and in the provincial cities. Their construction may be gathered from their numerous remains, and from the descriptions of them en by Roman writers; they resembled the Turkish and Etus ian baths. The essential parts of a Soman bath were as follows. — 1. The hypocaust, or stove, in the basement- story, for heating both the bath-rooms and the water. The water was contained in three receptacles or boilers, so arranged that the undermost, i'iiii: diately over the lire, contained the hot water; the one in the middle, the tepid water; and the uppermost, the cold water. These vessels were bo connected by pipes, both with the bath-rooms and with one another, that the hot water that (lowed from the lowest boiler was replaced by tepid water from the one above; and that, again, by cold from the uppermost — 2. The apodytervwm, or room for undressing. '■'. The frigidarium, a room with a basin for cold bathing. — 4. The tepidariu/m, the purpose of which cannot be exactly determined, but which seems to have been intended for bathing ill tepid water, and also for allowing the body to cool down in a mild temperature. — 5. The caldarium , in which sometimes the sudatio, or sweating- bath, and sometimes the real hot-water bath, were taken. This room had hollow walls, and the floor rested on low pillars over the hypocaust, so that it was surrounded on all sides with heated air. The liieoiuiun, which is spoken of as a part of the caldarium, was probably a kind of stove that was heated from the hypocaust, and contributed to

raise the temperature. In the bath-rooms there were basins (afvei) for holding the water, and rotmd Che Malls were benches or seats, which, in the caldarium, were raised as in an amphitheatre, in order to give the bathers the choice of the higher temperature of the upper part of the room, or of the more moderate of the lower. The caldarium contained also a labrwm or vase of several feet diameter, filled with cold water, into which the bathers dipped after the Lot hath. With these essential parts of Roman Bath, from a Painting on the Walls of the Thcnna; of Titus at Borne. a bath, there were usually connected an iinctiiariiim or elcEOtheaium — i.e., an anointing-room, and often gardens, covered walks, rooms for games, &c. The process of bathing was this : After undress- ing in the apodyterium, the bather was anointed in the eheotheaiam with a cheap coarse oil, and then pro* Led to a spacious apartment devoted to exercises of various kinds, among which games at ball held a prominent place (hence the hall was called spTuBrielerium). After exercise, he went into the caldarium, either merely to sweat or to take the hot bath; and during this part of the process, the body was scraped with instruments called etrigiles. Bi in : now dried with cloths, and slightly anointed all over with perfumed oils, ho resumed his dress, and thin passed a short time successively in the tepidarium and the frigidarium, which softened the transition from the great heat of the caldarium into the open air. The public baths for women were of similar construction, and were much frequented even by the most respectable. The women bathed in company, like the men. The irregularity of men and women bathing together is also alluded to by ancient writers; ami in later times, the baths in general became the scenes of all sorts of debauchery, as was the esse at Baite, The most remarkable remains of Roman baths are those of the baths of Titus, of Caracatla, and of Diocletian in Home, and the recently excavated therms at Pompeii : remains of the kind are also to be found in (Jermany, I'Yance, and Kngland. The extent and magnificence of those edifices it is difficult for us now to conceive. Speaking of the baths of ( 'araealla. Mr PergUSSOn, in his II, < qf A rchitecture, says : 'St. ( leorge's Hall, at Liverpool, is the most exact copy, in modern tunes, of a part of these baths. The hall itself is a reproduction, both in scale ami design, of tin- central hall of Caracalla'a baths, but improved in detail and design, having live bays instead of only three. With the two courts at each end, it makes up a suite of apartments Very similar to those found in the Roman examples. The whole building, however, is less than one fourth of the si/e of the central mass of a Roman bath, and therefore gives but little idea of the magnificence of the whole.' The ancient Hermans seem, according to Tacitus and other writers, to have been fondest of the cold river bath. When Roman luxury was driven out by German habits, and the north of Europe the upper-hand of the south, baths cease. 1 to be of public importance, and amid the tempestuous irruptions and fluctuations of the different nations, those splendid edifices fell into ruins. ( hristianity, however , by the institution of baptism, had pri for the bath its religious Signification ; and in the middle ages, among the ccren ies preceding the solemnity of conferring the honour of I the bath was held essential. The Arabians ami the Mohammedans generally had more completely adopted bathing into their manners and customs. Islam enjoins on the believer the careful pi ration of corporal purity ; and lor this pui Ins repeated daily ablutions. Besides certain circumstances and times make the use of the B. ritually obligatory on both men and women. Far this end, not only did the rich erect splendid baths in their houses and '.'\rdens, but bath-houses for the people in general were established in every town in which there was a mosque. The public baths of the Turks of the present day are a copy of those ancient Arabian baths. The eon those oriental balks, imitations of which are now t" be found in some European cities, is as follows: The building is of stone, the bath-rooms have a floor of marble, which is heated from below, ami tubes in the walls conduct the heat in all directions. The bather undresses, wraps himself in a blanket, puts on woollen slippers, to proved him from tie' heat of the Ho,, I-, and enters the bath-room. Here a general perspiration soon bn '• trough the skin, which is washed ,,|1 with cold water. The body is then rubbed with woollen cloths, and smeared with a soap or salve beneficial to the skin. This is generally accompanied by the operation of - The bath-attendant stretches the bather on a table, pours warm water over him, and then begins to press, squeeze, and twist his whole body with wonderful dexterity. Every limb is straightened and Stretched, and when he has finished one side, he begins on the other. Jle kneels upon the bather; he Seizes him by the Bhoulders, makes his backbone crack, and every vertebra quiver, or applies soft

blows to the flashy parts. He then takes a haircloth , and cube the whole body, rubs off the hard skin of the fiit with pumice-stone, anoints the bather with Map and perfumes, and Sni ting his hail and beard. This treatment lasts some three-quarters <>f an hour ; and the feeling after it is as of being born anew. An inexpressibly delicious (em of comfort p body, and soon ends in a .sweet sleep. After bathing, people in a cooler room, stretched on couches, and finally . sherbet, or lemonade. In England, France, and Germany, public i liahments for bathing were long unknown. It was during the Crusades, which brought the 1 1 and West into contact, that Europeans first became acquainted with the baths of the Asiatics; and the want of such institutions came to be more sensibly felt from the leprosy and other skin- diseases which intercourse with Asia introduced into Western Europe. The evil was at first sought to be met by establishing hospitals; but as the fi mud insufficient, baths and bath-rooms were erected, which gradually became public establishments. Besides the kinds of baths already described, there are now to be found in the larger cities of Europe, generally in connection with water-baths, imitations of the vapour-baths which have been long in common use in Russia* The R\ Bath consists of a small apartment built of wood, with broad benches running round it, on which the people lie undressed. By throwing water upon glowing hot pebbles, a dense hot steam is produced, which envelops the bathers, and throws them into such a heat, that the perspiration breaks out over the whole body. In this atmosphere of steam, the thermometer often rises to 1 12° — 140° F. After they have sweated for some time, and from time to time cooled themselves again, by having .iter ] mured over them, the skin is rubbed with soap, and with towels made of inner bark, or with brushes; they are Hogged with softened birch-twigs, and then washed with tepid, and afterwards with cold water ; and at last have cold water dashed over them. A bather will also go direct from the sweating-bath , and plunge into a river or a pond, or roll himself in the snow. These baths are a necessary of life in Russia, and are to be found in every village. The German vapour-bath differs in this, that the steam is produced in a boiler, and that the bather remains for some time in an adjoining room of moderate temperature, wrapped in blankets, to allow the perspiration to go on, and the blood to become calm. A ruder kind of sweating-bath, in a hole in the earth, or in a baking-oven, is practised among many nations ; among the Finns, the natives of -Mexico and South America, &c. As regards detergenoe, the vapour-bath is the only kind of bath that is really effectual. l naked in a room tilled with hot vapour (which produces no inconvenience in breathing), the scurf, which, notwithstanding all sorts of previous ablutions , has accumulated on the skin, is gradually softened and loosened, and is rubbed off in a surprising manner by the hands of the bath-man who is in attendance at these establishments. As in the Turkish bath, the person is cooled down by l»ing dashed with tepid and cold water. After this kind of bathing, the sensation is exceedingly agreeable. The process just mentioned may be said to resemble that in use by the Romans ; the hands of the operator having much the same effect as the atriijilfs of the ancients. Few of the ordinary bathing establishments in Great Britain have vapour- baths, at least not on a proper footing; and tie- great value of this species of bath as a purifier of the skin is little known. 710 Bathing is a very important agent in the preservation and restoration of health. Resides promoting cleanliness, the refreshing and invigorating effects of cold bathing in its various forms nave always been more or less understood, as ban the soothing effects of the warm bath. But the virtues of water as a curative agent have fully developed in modern times, since the i the system of therapeutics known as the water-cure or hydropathy. With that i i which i incident to everything new, the first promoters of this system gave it out as a panacea 'for all the ills that flesh is heir to.' But now that these quackish pretensions are all but universally given up, it is very generally admitted that water is capable of a large range of ell., be, soma of them apparently of the most lands; while the mode of action is nothing mysterious, but capable of explanation on the recognised principles of physi- ology'. The fuller exposition of this part of the subject will be more conveniently considered mider li', DBOPATHY. A Medicated Bath is one in which some substance , intended to act as a medicine, lias been mixed with the liquid. This is one of the most important methods known to medical art of bringing remedies to bear upon the system. The skin is by no means impervious to foreign substances ; and no other organ presents at once so large a surface to the matter to be imbibed ; at times, also, the other channels by which remedies are introduced into the body cannot be used. Baths of this kind are partly imitations of natural mineral waters, and partly other remedial mixtures. The mineral substances used are common salt, chloride of lime, nitric acid, corrosive sublimate, potash or soda caustic or carbonated , ashes, soap, iodine, sulphur, iron, &c. ; the vegetable are wine, vinegar, solutions of essential- oils, infusions of thyme, rosemary, lavender, wormwood , willow, oak, and Peruvian bark, &c. ; such animal substances as milk, blood, bouillon of meat, &c, are also sometimes employed as baths, with a view to impart nourishment, but whether much is taken up into the system, is doubtful. In the case, also, of vapour-baths, medicaments are added to the water with good effect; these must, of com volatile. If the whole body is to be immersed in the vapour, nothing must be used that might injure the organs of respiration ; when the application is partial, and by a special apparatus, this precaution is less necessary. In connection with this may be mentioned the so-called Smoke-baths, or medicated fumigations, in which the whole body, with exception , of course, of the head, or particular parts of it, arc brought in contact with the vapours of dry medicinal substances. Resinous aromatic substances, incense, myrrh, benzoin, amber, sulphur, cinnabar, and mercury are used for this purpose. The application must be made in what is called a fumigatmg- box, in which the particular part of the body alone is enclosed along with the vapour, in order that the respiratory organs may not be incommoded. The utmost precaution is requisite with the vapours of sulphur and mercury, as they are apt to occasion serious accidents. Another species of vapour-bath is what is called an ANIMAL Bath, which was known to the ancients, and was in great reputation in cases of lameness. Either the whole body of the patient is wrapped in the skin of a newly slaughtered animal, or an open ing is made, and the diseased limb inserted into the breast or belly of the animal while yet alive, or into the newly drawn blood. Sometimes smaller animals are killed, split up, and immediately applied to the diseased part. Of Gas Baths, the most generally used are those

of sulphuretted hydrogen and carbonic acid gas, which are to be had at certain mineral springs. The first, mixed in small quantity with atmospheric air, lowers the irritability of the air-tubes, and affords relief in many diseases of the respiratory organs. A stronger mixture of it, brought in contact with the miter surface, is of use in d Arising front depression of the functions of the skin. Carbonic acid gas gives a gentle stimulus to the skin, promotes menstruation, and is much u -d in many in the form of half-baths. In recent times, at lschl and other places, the vapours that arise from the mineral springs loaded with saline particles, are received in close rooms, in which the patients walk about, and allow the vapours to act upon the lungs and skin. The terms water-haih and mmd-lath have been adopted in chemistry, to signify a contrivance by which vessels that are to lie heated to a certain temperature are not brought into immediate contact with the fire, but receive their heat through tie medium of hot sand or water, so that the heating takes place uniformly, and overheating is avoided.

BATHS AND WA'SH-HOUSES, PoBLIO. The last few years have witnessed the erection of a number of public establishments, at which the masses may enjoy a bath for the merest trillo of their weekly earnings. Where steam-engines are employed in connection with cotton- factories or other works, there is usually a certain quantity of waste steam or waste hot water at disposal, which could, at an insignificant cost, be directed into baths for the use of the workmen of the establishment We are aware of one instance where seven baths were comfortably fitted up at the small expense of £'S0, in which the men and women bathe on alternate days, to the number of from thirty to eighty a week — paying a mere trillo to the keeper, who attends an hour and a half each evening , and finds towels, soap, &e., nothing being ed by the proprietors for the original outlay. But this is only a small part of the cure for a great evil. Where the masses are densely packed in lanes and alleys, where house-accommodation is dear and limited, where the necessaries of life have to be continually struggled for, and these conventional evils increased, in too many instances, by improvidence — the house is but a night-shelter, affording little or no convenience for the necessary operations of the housewife. Independent of this, a public wash-house is, in point of economy, preferable to any number of isolated efforts. By co-operation, superior accommodation, better apparatus, and a cheaper and more satisfactory result can be obtained; and thus the public wash-house, where self-paying and self-supported, may be classed among the co-operative arrangements which characterise the social features of the age. Mrs Catherine Wilkinson of Liverpool, in a year of cholera, bravely offered the use of her small house, and the value of her personal superintendence , to her poorer neighbours, to facilitate the washing of their clothes at a time when cleanliness was more than usually important. The success attending the exertions of a single individual led to the formation of a benevolent society, and ultimately to important municipal arrangements. In IS44, a public meeting was held at the Mansion House, attended by many persons of wealth and influence, to encourage the formation of B. and W. in London; hence resulted an 'Association for Promoting Cleanliness amongst the Poor.' Independently of this movement, a reform had already been commenced by a 'Committee for the Houseless Poor,' who, among other things, purchased or rented an old roomy building in Glasshouse Yard, surrounded by the poor and dense population of the London Docks district. A bath-house and a wash-house were fitted up ; baths, cisterns, boilers, cold and hot water, towels, soap, soda, were provided; and the poor avited to come in, and wash and bathe without expense to themselves. There were also provided pails, brushes, and whitewash, to those who would take the trouble to give a little cleanliness to their poor dwellings. This was effected mainly through the benevolent exertions of Mr Bowie, a surgeon, who applied himself with earnestness t i the subject. The association, afterwards founded at the city meeting, sought two objects — to induce a wish for cleanliness among the poor ; and to render public B. and W. self-paying, as a guarantee for their pennanency. Having obtained plans and estimates from architects, the association built a model establishment in Goulston Square, White-chapel; but the outlay unfortunately reached £26,000. In the meantime, another society had succeeded in • fishing B. anil W. in George Street, Hampstead Road, favoured by a liberal arrangement on the part of the New lliver Company in the supply of water: this establishment was opened in August 1846. In the same year, parliament passed an act to enable borough-councils and parish vestries to establish public B. and W., supported by borough ami parish rates, if the householders should sanction such a proceeding. In 1847, another act strengthened the former ; and the two together contain the necessary clauses for defining the details of the plan (see the following article). The parish of St Martin's-in-the-Fields was the first to take advantage of the new act; and before the close of 1892; six parishes had erected public B. and W. At the beginning of 1856, the list had nearly doubled. The original free but humble building in Glasshouse Yard had been abandoned; but the model cstabbsh- ment in Goulston Square, and the separate undertaking in Hampstead Koad, remained. There are, in 1873, about sixteen of these public and parochial B. and W. in the metropolis. It is not to be supposed that these efforts have been confined to London. Liverpool took precedence in date, and has since worthily maintained her interest in the matter. Manchester, Oldham, Hull, Bristol, Birmingham, Preston, Bath, Wolverhampton, Coventry, Plymouth, Chester, Sunderland, ! Macclesfield, Oxford, Maidstone, Exeter, K ham, Colchester, South Shields, Dublin, B Glasgow, Dundee, Aberdeen, and other towns, have since adopted a similar course; and it may safely be predicted that borough and parochial B. and W. will increase in number year by year; for if they do not actually pay their full expenses at the low tariff charge, the deficiency will be so small as to 1 ie practically unf elt by ratepayers. When the legislature took up the subject, the purpose of the committee appointed in 184(1 was in great part answered ; but that committee continued to exist until 1856; and the exertions of its mem- ln is were attended with very beneficial results, in drawing the attention of influential persons in various countries to the advantages of public B. and W The French government voted 000,000 francs to assist the promotion of such institutions in France, after the plan of the model establishment; and a scheme was set on foot for i nrteen establishments in Paris, for which 2,000,000 francs would be required. The municipality of Venice marked out an expenditure of £33,000 in the erection of B. on the same plan. The Norwegian government applied to the committee far 'Uw puna, &c, of their wash-house at Goulston Square, as a guide for the erection of one at Christiania ; and a subscription was made for the erection of B. and \V. 7«

,'t Copenhagen, The Belgian government, and the authorities at Hamburg, Turin, Munich, Amsterdam , Lisbon, New York, and other places, were in like maimer furnished with information on the subject In nearly all the London establishments, which may also be taken as types of those in the country, the characteristic features arc as follows: The h. for males and females are on opposite sides of the building, She separate IX, in large well I and well-ventilated rooms, are shut in by walls, rally of slate; and the B. themselves, supplied with fifty or sixty gallons of water for each bather, are either of zinc or enamelled iron. There are two, three, or four classes of B., charged differently according to the amount of accoinnio afforded. At the St Martin's establishment, where there arc only two classes of I'.., it has been found that the second-class bathers are thrice as numerous as the first. Arrangements, slightly varying in different establishments, afford means for conveying hot and cold water to every bath. Iu some instances, there are tepid as will as cold swimming or plunging B. ; while two or three of them afford t for shower and vapour baths. The washing-rooms, in most of these establishments, are provided with numerous small compartments, doorless and roofli each for one person. Each compartment contains a boiler and a washing-tub, with taps for hot water, cold water, waste water, and steam: all unlimited in quantity, wilful waste of course being guarded against. An American washing-board assists the operations; and a rack-work stand protects the feet. The steam from all the compartments is carried upwards to one great ventilating shaft. The 'wringing' of the wet washed linen is effected by putting the articles into a sort of perforated cylinder, which is then rotated with great velocity; the centrifugal force drives out the water through the perforations and interstices, leaving the linen, though damp, much drier than it can be made by the familiar laundry process. The clothes are then taken to the drying-room, where they are hung on frames or 'horses' in small chambers heated with hot air to about 200° or 210°. 10,000 articles of V, clothing can now be dried with about £1 worth of fuel, or much less in the towns of the north. In some of the improved establishments, there is a lining compartment belonging to each wa compartment, effecting a manifest saving of time to the washers; in some of them, too, there is an ironing-board to each compartment; but the general plan is to have a large ironing-room, well provided with irons, ironing-blankets ami boards, and heating arrangements. The charge is from Id. to °J.</. per hour, according to the class and the accommoilat ion. One particular establishment at Manchester may usefully be described more in detail, as a type of the general class of B. and \Vr. There is a men's swimming-bath, 70 feet by 25, with a pavement of polishi il York stone on a foundation of concrete and cement; the sides are of porcelain tiles laid in cement. There are 32 enclosed dressing-closets. Over these, on iron pillars, arc 17 men's warm baths, each 8 feet by 7. Separated from this gallery by an open passage are f> extra first I baths, larger in size, and having shower-baths. There is a second-class swimming-bath nearly like that for the first-class; with its gallery of small baths over. The wromen's baths, iu a different part of the building, comprise 4 first and 7 second class. The laundry is at one end of the building. The washing-room is 64 feet by 38; it comprises 6 first-class and 30 second-class compartments, each of the former provided with three tubs, and each of the latter with two. 718 There is provision for drying any amount of clothes in twenty minutes after tin- washing and writ mpleted, All tin- women bave access to two patent wringing-maohines. There is an ironing- room adjoining, fitted up with stoves, The water- tank has a capacity of 3000 gallons; the baths, if all full, would bold 60,000 gallons. Since the taking up of tins subject by the municipal authorities of various towns, there have I n v. reliable statistics obtainable relating to the extent to which these valuah omenta arc used: but it is known that the I'.. and \V. e li bed by the several parishes either pay their oi 1 ing expenses wholly, or approach so near to it as to encroach very little on the parish rates, I hie satisfactory feature connected with the system is, that when the local authorities are slow to tablish ft and W., wealthy manufacturers or townsmen often take up the matter at their own expense, and then leave the ratepayers nothing iodo than to provide the small balance of annual working accounts. As an example of free baths for men and boys (without washhouses), may be cited the establishment opened at Derby in June lsT-'i, and presented to the corporation by Mr Ball, .M.I', for the borough. It comprises two swimming- baths, one for men and one for boys, each Ion feet Ion by 60 in width. There arc 57 half-closed dressing-boxes around the men's bath, and 72 open boxes around the boys'. The two baths together hold 200,000 gallons of water, which is renewed once a week. The least satisfactory part of the system in its practical operation, is that which relates to the wash- houses. Laundresses, boarding and lodging house keepers, and families in the middle ranks of life, use these W. rather than really poor families; they do : ' I use the expense is very low. not because they are unable to pay higher. It is sometimes believed that those for whose benefit the system was established are ashamed to bring their scanty, coarse, and much-worn apparel to a place where it may meet the eyes of others: if this be so, surely a remedy might be applied ! BATHS and WASH -HOUSES, Acts emi :\iii.im:. The establishment of public B. and W. is regulated in England and Wales by two acts of parliament — the 0 and 10 Vict. c. 74, and lo and 11 Vict. c. 61 — which arc to In' considered as one act. The sanitary regulations so legalised are merely permissive, and in no respect made compulsory on the public; but their wisdom, benevolence , and consideration for the health of the people, strongly recommend their adoption. The provisions of the act may be adopted for any incorporated borough, or for any parish not within any such incorporated borough; subject, however, in tho case of a parish, to the approval of one of Her Majesty's principal secretaries of state. In tho case of a borough, the adoption of the act is left to the discretion of the council of the borough ; and the expense is to be charged upon the borough fund, the council being empowered to levy, either as part of the borough rate, or by a separate rate, such sums as may from time to time be necessary. In the case, again, of a parish, it is left to the vestry, with the sanction of one of the secretaries of state, to decide on the adoption of the act ; and in such case, the vestry shall appoint not less than three, and not more than seven persons, rate] layers, to be Commissioners for carrying out the provisions of the act. Regulations for the proceedings of these commissioners are prescribed in the act. The expense is to be charged upon the poor-rate. The vestries of any two or more parishes may concur in carrying out the act.

The act contains numerous other provisions and regulations relating to the facilities required for the tions of the -uncils and parish com- uers: thus, they may barrow money -with the approval of the Treasury; they may have money advanced to them by the Public Works Loan • "in- mission rs ; they may avail the mserves of the Railway Companies Clauses Consolidation Act of 1846 for certain limited purposes, such as borrowing money on mortgage, the accountability of officers of the company, the making of by-laws subject to other provisions, and the recovery of damages and penalties. After these preliminary facilities, the act proto specify the powers of the borough councils and parish commissioners, as to erection or purchase of buildings, &c, for the purposes contemplated. Among other things, it is provided that the number of baths and the number of washing-tubs for the labouring-classes shall not be less than twice the number of those for any higher class ore] The council and commissioners respectively are empowered to make by-laws for regulating the use of the B. and W., which, howi not be enforced until they have been approved by a tary of state.
